title: Contracts II: Performance, Breach and Remedies
description: Continue Contracts I by analyzing conditions, performance, breach, excuse and third-party rights. Four modules combine original worked problems with alternative damages calculations and a complete fictional breach memorandum, model analysis and self-assessment rubric.
author: Erudior
disclaimer: Independent educational preparation only; not legal advice, university credit, a J.D. degree or bar eligibility. Numbered exercise rules are expressly stipulated teaching assumptions, not a national contract code or the law of a fictional real jurisdiction. Actual primary-law readings are identified separately. Writing tasks are self-assessed, not automatically graded.

modules.title: Expectation, reliance, restitution and equitable relief

lessons.title: Separate promises from conditions
lessons.body:
Contracts I asked whether an enforceable agreement exists and what its terms mean. Here we assume formation unless a problem says otherwise. Our first question is narrower: has a particular duty become due? A valid contract can exist even though a condition to payment has not occurred. Conversely, a payment may be due despite a defect that gives the payer a separate damages claim. Keeping those propositions separate prevents the common mistake of treating every disappointment as permission to walk away.

Use P1–P4 in the performance reference for this lesson. These are stipulated exercise rules, deliberately bounded so you can practice analysis. Actual courts may interpret the language or allocate burdens differently. All persons and transactions in the worked problems are fictional. The primary reading at the end illustrates why a lawyer must read the particular clause instead of replacing it with a slogan.

## Identify the event and the duty

A **[[promise]]** is a commitment to act or refrain from acting. A **[[condition]]** is an uncertain event whose occurrence, unless excused, controls a duty. Write the event and the controlled duty in separate columns. “The artist promises to submit sketches Friday” states a commitment. “The final payment is due only if the committee approves the sketches” connects an event to payment. One clause can contain both a commitment and a condition, but you must explain both functions.

A **[[condition precedent]]** must occur before the controlled duty becomes due. In a concurrent exchange, each side may need to offer its own performance before demanding the other's. **[[Tender]]** means an offer of the required performance, made with the ability and readiness to perform under the exercise assumptions. A buyer who neither brings payment nor offers it cannot simply accuse a ready seller of refusing a simultaneous exchange.

An **[[express condition]]** comes from the agreement's terms. P1 treats unmistakable conditional language as requiring the specified event, subject to P2 excuses. An ordinary promised completion date is not automatically an express condition of all payment. For ambiguous language, P1 prefers a promise over a forfeiture-producing express condition. This is an interpretation rule for these exercises, not permission to erase clear terms.

## Nonoccurrence and breach answer different questions

Suppose a grant agreement says a museum will pay a stipend only if an outside sponsor awards funding. If nobody promised to obtain that award, its failure may leave the payment duty inactive without anyone breaching a promise. The museum's disappointment does not create a damages claim against the applicant. A separate promise to submit the funding application would create a separate issue if the applicant never applied.

For each clause, ask three questions. What event was required? Did anybody undertake to make that event happen? What consequence follows from its absence? The first concerns conditions, the second concerns promises, and the third concerns relief. A good analysis may conclude that payment is not due but that a distinct promise was breached. Avoid collapsing those conclusions into “the contract is void.”

A **[[constructive condition]]** is a dependency supplied by the exercise framework rather than expressly stated. P3 generally links the other side's remaining services duties to substantial performance. The next lesson explains that rule. It does not replace P1's treatment of an expressly conditioned payment with a percentage-completion test.

## Excuses require their own facts

P2 recognizes **[[prevention]]** when a party wrongfully hinders the event that controls its own duty. The party cannot simply rely on the nonoccurrence it caused. Identify the required cooperation, the obstructing conduct, and causation. A payer who refuses an agreed inspection appointment may have prevented a certificate. A payer who refuses an appointment outside the agreed period has not necessarily done so.

A **[[waiver]]** is the intentional relinquishment of a condition's protection. Under P2, a clear waiver of a condition benefiting the waiving party can excuse it. The rule does not authorize one party to waive a condition protecting somebody else. Before reliance, reinstatement may sometimes be possible with reasonable notice and time to comply; these exercises state the relevant facts. A sudden demand after detrimental reliance is not treated as an automatic restoration.

**[[Forfeiture]]** describes the loss of a substantial earned exchange because of a failed condition. P2 permits consideration of disproportionate forfeiture only when the event was not a material part of the agreed exchange. Do not assume every harsh result is excused. A genuine safety approval central to the bargain can matter differently from a minor paperwork detail. Explain the competing interests before predicting a result.

### Example 1: A certificate blocked by the payer

Mira agrees to restore a hall for 12,000 dollars. Final payment is expressly conditioned on the owner's inspection certificate. The contract requires the owner to inspect within two days of a timely request. Mira completes the work and requests inspection Monday. The owner admits the work is satisfactory but refuses inspection solely to avoid paying.

First identify the event: issuance of the inspection certificate. Second identify the controlled duty: final payment. Third apply P2: the owner owed cooperation, deliberately withheld it, and caused the missing certificate. Under the stipulated prevention rule the owner cannot use that absence to defeat payment. This does not prove the work was defect-free in every case; that fact is supplied here. If a defect existed, its separate consequences would still require analysis.

### Example 2: A funding condition with no promise to fund

An arts group promises a 2,000-dollar travel stipend only if an independent foundation awards a named grant. The group expressly undertakes no duty to secure the award. The foundation declines despite a complete application. Neither party obstructed the process or waived the condition.

Identify the event as the grant award, not submission of an application. The event did not occur, and the facts supply no excuse. The stipend duty therefore does not mature under P1. There is no separate broken promise to obtain funding. Change one fact: the group promised to submit the application and deliberately discarded it. Now investigate both breach of that promise and prevention; do not merely recycle the original conclusion.

## Practice a short analysis

Draft four sentences about a caterer whose payment depends on a fire inspection. Identify who controls the inspection and whether the contract requires cooperation. State two missing facts that could change your conclusion. Then revise the clause to make timely inspection a promise instead of an express condition. Describe how that change could affect payment and damages separately.

The exercise is self-assessed. Compare your draft with P1–P2, not with an invented universal rule. A complete answer names the duty, event, evidence of occurrence, possible excuse, and consequence. It does not award damages before identifying a broken promise and a supported loss.

## Primary reading

Read the condition discussion in [National Fuel Gas Distribution Corp. v Hartford Fire Insurance Co., 2005 NY Slip Op 52274(U)](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2005/2005_52274.htm). Identify its court and procedural setting, then distinguish an express condition from an interpretive preference. This is a reported New York trial-court decision quoting higher authority, not the higher-court opinion itself or a nationwide rule.

## Common mistakes

- Calling every contractual deadline a condition of all payment.
- Treating a failed outside event as a breach by a party who never promised it.
- Invoking prevention without identifying wrongful interference and causation.
- Using substantial performance to ignore a clear, unexcused express condition.

## Key points

- Separate the event from the duty it controls.
- Analyze promises and conditions independently even when they share a clause.
- Support waiver, prevention and forfeiture arguments with particular facts.
- State whether a duty matured before deciding what remedy follows.

lessons.title: Evaluate defective performance and available responses
lessons.body:
An installer finishes a large job but leaves one damaged handle. A seller delivers a shipment containing the wrong model. Both performances are defective, yet the permitted response may differ. This lesson develops a disciplined way to evaluate the seriousness of a defect and distinguish the services framework from selected sales rules. Begin with classification, then identify the relevant promise and any express condition from the previous lesson.

P3 governs the ordinary services problems here. P4 supplies a limited comparison for a single-delivery goods contract. Neither rule covers every construction contract, installment sale, warranty or accepted-goods dispute. When the facts identify a special framework, use it. The purpose is to learn which additional question to ask, not to memorize “minor defects always count” or “minor defects never count.”

## Assess materiality in context

A **[[material breach]]** substantially undermines the promised exchange under P3. Consider the benefit denied to the injured party, whether money can compensate, the forfeiture termination would impose, the likelihood of prompt cure, and good faith. These are considerations, not a five-point tally. A missing safety feature can outweigh many completed cosmetic details. An easily repaired scratch may have a very different significance.

**[[Substantial performance]]** means performance sufficient to satisfy the constructive condition of the other side's return duty, while leaving liability for remaining defects. It does not mean perfect performance or forgiveness. Under P3, a substantially performing service provider may recover the due price subject to an appropriate offset for proven deficiencies. Calculate the offset only after identifying the proper measure of loss.

A **[[partial breach]]** leaves remaining performance obligations in place under our exercises, while permitting compensation for loss. A material failure may justify **[[suspension]]**, a temporary withholding of remaining performance while the failure remains uncured. A **[[total breach]]** justifies treating remaining duties as discharged under the stipulated facts. Do not treat suspension and discharge as synonyms. Whether a material failure has become total can depend on delay, cure prospects and the time-sensitive purpose.

## Ask what cure changes

**[[Cure]]** means correcting the deficient performance in the time and manner the governing rule allows. A prompt, reliable repair proposal may reduce the justification for ending a services agreement, but a promise of eventual repair does not erase an immediate serious loss. If an emergency exit remains blocked on the day of a public event, a repair next month does not supply the benefit due today.

Keep evidence contemporaneous. Record what was missing, when the other party learned of it, what correction was offered and whether the proposed correction could preserve the bargain. Under P3, a party that treats a readily curable, minor omission as a total breach risks becoming the party that wrongfully refuses performance. The lesson's questions state whether an express condition exists so that this separate issue does not hide inside the problem.

For damages, a reasonable repair cost often measures a defect, but an economically wasteful reconstruction can raise a different measure. The selected rule asks whether correction is grossly disproportionate to the actual benefit and whether the promised feature had a supported special purpose. A named finish essential to a historic restoration is not interchangeable merely because another finish looks similar to a contractor.

## Compare goods carefully

The **[[perfect tender]]** starting point in P4 lets a buyer reject a nonconforming single delivery before acceptance, subject to the stated agreement and sales-law qualifications. It is not the substantial-performance rule. However, rejection must be timely and notified under the exercise assumptions, and the seller may have a right to cure. These procedural details matter as much as spotting a mismatch.

P4 allows a seller, after timely notice, to make a conforming delivery within the unexpired contract time. A separate rule can allow further reasonable time where the seller reasonably believed the original tender would be acceptable. Questions using that second situation expressly provide the necessary facts. Do not infer an unlimited extension from the seller's preference.

**[[Acceptance of goods]]** is distinct from accepting an offer to form a contract. Once goods are accepted, ordinary rejection is no longer the same available route. **[[Revocation of acceptance]]** has separate requirements, including substantial impairment and other conditions not developed fully here. Installment contracts also use a distinct substantial-impairment framework. Those boundaries prevent P4 from becoming an all-purpose cancellation rule.

### Example 1: A small defect in completed services

Jules finishes a 10,000-dollar shelving installation. One handle has an accidental scratch, repair costs 100 dollars, the shelves are safe and usable, and no express condition makes flawless handles a condition of payment. The owner refuses the entire price and demands demolition.

Under P3, almost all the expected benefit is present, compensation is easy, and prompt cure is realistic. These facts support substantial performance and a partial breach. With repair cost stipulated as the proper measure, the net amount due is 9,900 dollars: 10,000 minus 100. The owner does not obtain a free installation. Nor does Jules obtain immunity from the defect merely by finishing most of the work.

### Example 2: A timely goods cure

A shop contracts for 100 blue folders delivered by Friday. On Tuesday the seller delivers red folders. The buyer immediately rejects and notifies the seller. The seller gives timely notice that it will replace them and delivers 100 conforming blue folders Thursday. The parties have no contrary term and this is not an installment contract.

Apply P4's single-delivery starting point: the red folders are nonconforming, so timely rejection is available. Then apply the cure rule: contract time remained, notice was timely, and conforming replacement arrived before Friday. The buyer cannot treat the first color mismatch alone as defeating the entire contract after this effective cure. The example does not resolve any separately proven loss from the initial tender; that question would require its own rule and facts.

## Build a response table

For a service dispute, make columns for defect, lost benefit, cure, compensation and proposed response. For a goods dispute, add delivery date, acceptance status, notification and cure deadline. These columns reveal why two superficially similar defects can justify different responses. They also expose missing facts without pretending every uncertainty prevents useful analysis.

Try changing the shelving example: the shelves tip over during ordinary use. Reassess deprivation and safety rather than assuming the same 100-dollar offset. Then change only the folder example's deadline to Monday before delivery. The ordinary within-time cure route is unavailable; investigate the separate further-time rule instead of announcing either automatic cure or automatic defeat.

## Primary reading

Read [Jacob & Youngs, Inc. v Kent, 230 NY 239 (1921)](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/archives/jacob_kent.htm), including the dissent. Identify the evidence the majority thought relevant and why the dissent objected. Compare [New York UCC § 2-601](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/UCC/2-601) and [§ 2-508](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/UCC/2-508). The opinion is a particular New York construction case; the statutes are New York enactments governing goods, not services.

## Common mistakes

- Counting completed tasks without evaluating the promised benefit.
- Treating substantial performance as a finding that no breach occurred.
- Turning temporary suspension into automatic permanent discharge.
- Applying perfect tender after acceptance without checking separate requirements.

## Key points

- Materiality depends on the exchange and the consequences of the defect.
- Substantial performance can coexist with damages.
- Cure, timing and notice can change the justified response.
- Classify the transaction and acceptance status before choosing a sales remedy.

lessons.title: Distinguish insecurity, repudiation and retraction
lessons.body:
A contract can be threatened before its performance date. One party may announce a refusal, make performance impossible by its own conduct, or merely disclose a troubling problem. The response should fit the evidence. Treating every anxious message as a final refusal can destroy an agreement that would have been performed. Ignoring a clear refusal can needlessly enlarge the eventual loss.

Use B1–B2 in the breach reference. B1 supplies the course's general anticipatory-breach assumptions. B2 supplies a limited goods-assurance comparison based on identified sales provisions. Do not assume that every jurisdiction gives a service customer the same statutory assurance procedure. When a question involves services, it expressly identifies any contractual assurance right.

## A refusal before the due date

**[[Anticipatory repudiation]]** is a sufficiently clear refusal or qualifying disabling act before a material future performance is due. Under B1, “I will not perform the agreed job” ordinarily qualifies. “I am worried about staffing, but I expect to finish” ordinarily raises uncertainty rather than a definite refusal. Context matters: a party's demand for an additional payment coupled with an unequivocal refusal to perform otherwise can communicate repudiation.

A **[[prospective breach]]** is the broader category of threatened future nonperformance. Not every prospective difficulty satisfies B1. Identify the particular performance, its due date, the communication or act, and why the expected loss is material. An inconsequential threatened omission is not automatically a repudiation of the entire exchange.

B1 allows the injured party to treat a qualifying repudiation as a basis for responding before the due date and to suspend remaining dependent performance. The injured party may seek an appropriate remedy or wait for a reasonable period under the exercise facts. This does not authorize accumulating avoidable losses indefinitely. The eventual damages analysis still asks what reasonable measures could have reduced the harm.

## Retraction depends on a timeline

**[[Retraction]]** is a clear withdrawal of repudiation accompanied by readiness to perform, including any justified assurance under the applicable rule. B1 allows it before the next performance is due unless the injured party has materially changed position, cancelled, or otherwise indicated that the repudiation is final. A counterparty need not abandon a reasonable replacement agreement simply because the original promisor changes its mind.

Build a timeline with at least four entries: the original due date, repudiation, the injured party's response, and attempted retraction. A text sent before a replacement contract may have a different effect from the same text sent afterward. Do not compress those dates into “they eventually said they would perform.”

Retraction is not an **[[accord]]**, an agreement to accept stipulated substitute performance in satisfaction of an existing duty, nor a **[[modification]]**, a change to the contract's terms. It concerns restoring the repudiating party's rights under the existing agreement, subject to the governing limits. An accord need not involve a disputed duty. The agreement is distinct from satisfaction, the rendering of the agreed substitute performance; do not treat the promise of later substitute performance as completed satisfaction. A proposed return only at a higher price may still fail to communicate performance of the original obligation.

## Assurance addresses justified insecurity

**[[Adequate assurance]]** is reliable evidence of future performance sufficient under the applicable circumstances. Under B2, reasonable grounds for insecurity in a goods contract can justify a written demand. The demanding party may commercially reasonably suspend performance for which it has not already received the agreed return. This is not permission to withhold an unrelated debt or impose new commercial terms.

Reasonable grounds require evidence, such as verified shutdown of the seller's only production line. Mere buyer's remorse is insufficient. Between merchants, commercial standards inform both the grounds and the adequacy of the response. A documented replacement-production arrangement may be more meaningful than an unsupported promise, but a demand for impossible security can exceed what the circumstances justify.

B2 follows the selected statute's reasonable-time limit, which cannot exceed thirty days. Thirty days is a ceiling, not a guaranteed waiting period in every transaction. A seasonal delivery due in a few days may demand a much faster adequate response. Failure to provide adequate assurance after a justified demand within the reasonable period counts as repudiation under the stipulated rule.

### Example 1: Retraction after replacement

On May 1 a designer states, “I will not deliver the agreed exhibit plan due June 1.” The plan is the agreement's central performance. On May 3 the museum reasonably signs a binding replacement contract. On May 4 the original designer says she can now perform the original deal.

The May 1 statement is clear and concerns material future performance, so B1 applies. The May 3 replacement materially changes the museum's position before the attempted retraction. Under B1, the designer cannot insist that the museum accept reinstatement. The museum still must support its damages and the reasonableness of its response. If the museum had only made a revocable inquiry, material change would require a different factual assessment.

### Example 2: A justified written demand

A buyer learns from verified records that a goods seller's only plant has closed. Delivery is due in three weeks. The buyer sends a written request for credible evidence of timely substitute production and commercially reasonably suspends its unpaid advance. Five days later the seller supplies a documented subcontract and confirmed capacity sufficient for timely delivery. The facts stipulate that this assurance is adequate under the trade's standards.

The closure supplies reasonable grounds; the demand addresses performance, not a better bargain. Adequate assurance arrives within the stipulated reasonable period. B2 does not allow the buyer to declare repudiation merely because thirty days have not passed or because it now prefers a cheaper seller. Its justified suspension ends when adequate assurance resolves the insecurity.

## Write a disciplined response recommendation

In a study memorandum, state what the communication establishes and what it leaves open. “This sounds bad” is not analysis. Specify whether you recommend requesting information, making a justified assurance demand, allowing a cure period, or treating a clear repudiation as final under the supplied assumptions. Explain what could change your recommendation.

Practice with a vendor saying, “Our driver quit; we are interviewing replacements and still plan delivery Friday.” Identify why the statement differs from “No delivery Friday, whatever happens.” Then add proof that the vendor sold the only custom-made item to another buyer. Consider whether conduct changes your assessment even though its latest message uses reassuring language.

The timing of remedial steps also matters. Document the replacement quote and why it was reasonable when obtained. Later hindsight does not necessarily establish that a sensible response was excessive. Conversely, an injured party cannot deliberately choose an extravagant substitute and assume every added cost transfers to the repudiator.

## Primary reading

Compare [New York UCC § 2-609](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/UCC/2-609), [§ 2-610](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/UCC/2-610), and [§ 2-611](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/UCC/2-611). Locate the written-demand language, reasonable-time ceiling, commercially reasonable waiting provision and limits on retraction. These are New York sales provisions; B1 remains an express teaching assumption for services. For a jurisdiction-specific comparison of an executory accord and its performance, read [New York General Obligations Law § 15-501](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GOB/15-501); its definition is not limited to disputed obligations, and its writing and enforcement rules are specific to that statute.

## Common mistakes

- Treating uncertainty as an unequivocal refusal without reading the full message.
- Giving every assurance demand a mandatory thirty-day waiting period.
- Ignoring a replacement commitment made before attempted retraction.
- Demanding a price concession under the label of assurance.

## Key points

- Separate insecurity from a qualifying repudiation.
- Tie suspension to the relevant dependent or unreturned performance.
- Use a dated timeline to analyze retraction.
- A justified assurance demand seeks reliable performance of the existing bargain.

lessons.title: Analyze changed circumstances and allocated risk
lessons.body:
Not every failure to perform is an unexcused breach. A later event may defeat an assumption essential to the agreement. But difficulty, cost and disappointment also occur within ordinary commercial risk. This lesson asks which circumstance changed, whose duty is affected, who bore that risk, and what consequence the selected rule permits. That sequence prevents the unhelpful conclusion that an event either excuses everyone or excuses nobody.

B3–B4 supply our stipulated exercise framework. Real jurisdictions differ in terminology, strictness and treatment of foreseeability. A case about a lease does not automatically establish a rule for a goods seller. A contract clause may allocate a risk differently from the background law. The exercise rules let you practice those distinctions while the primary readings show where further research would begin.

## Separate three kinds of interference

**[[Impossibility]]** concerns performance that the qualifying event makes objectively impossible under B3, such as destruction of a specified, irreplaceable subject without fault. Distinguish impossibility from one promisor's inability to afford performance. If ordinary equivalent supplies remain readily available, “my preferred supplier failed” does not by itself establish objective impossibility.

**[[Impracticability]]** concerns extraordinary difficulty or expense of the stipulated qualifying kind, not merely a bargain that became less profitable. B3 asks whether nonoccurrence of the event was a basic assumption, whether the party was without fault, and whether the party or agreement allocated the risk to that party. No fixed percentage cost increase automatically decides our questions.

**[[Frustration of purpose]]** concerns a substantially destroyed principal purpose, recognized by both sides, even though literal performance may remain possible. Suppose a room is rented solely to view a named procession and both parties understand that purpose. Cancellation of the procession presents a different issue from destruction of the room. In the first, the promised room remains usable but the shared purpose may have vanished.

The defenses are related but not interchangeable. A disappointed private plan is not necessarily the contract's mutually recognized principal purpose. A restaurant's falling sales do not establish that supplying its ordinary premises has become impossible. Identify the event's effect on the particular duty or purpose rather than choosing a doctrine from the event's dramatic label.

## Read allocation before invoking background rules

**[[Risk allocation]]** assigns responsibility for a contingency through agreement or the governing framework. A fixed price often allocates ordinary cost variation, while an explicit clause may address extraordinary events. Read precisely: a promise to obtain all permits may matter when a permit is refused, but its scope must be interpreted. Do not assume that naming a task necessarily assigns every imaginable related risk.

A **[[force majeure clause]]** is an agreement provision addressing specified disruptive events and their consequences. Under B4, inspect the listed events, any catchall, the causal connection to nonperformance, exclusions, notice requirements, mitigation duties and stated relief. A clause granting a ten-day extension does not automatically grant permanent discharge or return every earlier payment.

Suppose a clause covers floods causing site closure but expressly excludes staffing shortages. A contractor who deliberately moves its crew to a more profitable project cannot invoke “unforeseen circumstances” to bypass that exclusion. Suppose instead an official flood order closes the only site. The clause may apply, but the contractor must still satisfy the stipulated notice and causation requirements.

## Match the consequence to the event

A **[[temporary impracticability]]** may justify delay rather than permanent discharge if later performance remains materially the same exchange under B3. If the date itself is central, a delay past that date may defeat the bargain. Always ask whether performance later would supply the contracted benefit. A delayed generic report differs from catering a wedding after the guests have left.

**[[Allocation of supply]]** arises in the selected goods comparison when a qualifying event affects only part of a seller's capacity. The seller must allocate fairly and reasonably under B3's goods rule and provide seasonable notice, including the estimated quota when required. Excuse is not a license to favor the highest bidder while abandoning the remaining customers without explanation.

Excuse of a future duty does not necessarily settle payments for benefits already conferred. **[[Restitution]]** may address retained benefits under a separate rule. Nor does a valid excuse automatically erase an earlier completed breach. Put each event on the timeline and identify what remained due when the later disruption occurred.

### Example 1: Ordinary price movement

A printer agrees to supply ordinary paper folders for 4,000 dollars. Paper costs rise by ten percent within normal market variation. Equivalent paper is readily available, and the fixed-price agreement contains no applicable adjustment clause. The printer refuses delivery and invokes impracticability.

B3 does not treat ordinary price movement as a qualifying extraordinary event. The cost increase lies within the stipulated allocated commercial risk, and performance remains available. The printer's desire to preserve its expected margin does not establish excuse. This conclusion depends on the supplied normal-market facts; a different disruption would require fresh analysis rather than a universal percentage threshold.

### Example 2: A vanished shared purpose

Eli rents a balcony solely to watch a one-time ceremonial procession. Both parties expressly identify that sole purpose. The procession is unexpectedly and permanently cancelled without either party's fault. The room remains accessible, no alternative contractual purpose exists, and neither party assumed the cancellation risk.

Literal use of the balcony remains possible, so impossibility is not the strongest label. Under B3, frustration is the stronger argument: the mutually recognized principal purpose has been substantially destroyed, noncancellation was a basic assumption, and risk was not allocated to Eli. Future performance may be discharged under the stipulated facts. Treatment of an advance payment is a separate restitution question, not proof that cancellation never mattered.

## Practice comparing changed facts

Change the balcony facts so Eli merely hoped to photograph a friend walking by, without telling the owner. Explain why a private objective weakens the frustration argument. Then change the written agreement to say that Eli bears procession-cancellation risk. The event is identical, but its legal allocation changes the result under B3.

Now consider a temporary government closure affecting a goods factory with two operating sites. Ask whether production can shift, whether the parties assumed a greater obligation, what allocation is fair, and what notice is required. Do not infer an excuse from the existence of an official order alone. The relationship between the order and this seller's actual delivery matters.

## Primary reading

Read [New York UCC § 2-615](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/UCC/2-615), especially its opening limitation, partial-capacity allocation and notice provisions. Compare the impossibility discussion in [A/R Retail LLC v Hugo Boss Retail, Inc., 2021 NY Slip Op 21139](https://www.nycourts.gov/Reporter/3dseries/2021/2021_21139.htm). The latter is a particular New York trial-court lease decision, not a universal hardship standard. Neither reading silently replaces B3–B4 in the exercises.

## Common mistakes

- Treating a bad bargain as automatic impracticability.
- Confusing a private motive with a shared principal purpose.
- Ignoring a contract's allocation or notice requirements.
- Assuming a temporary event always permanently discharges the agreement.

## Key points

- Identify the affected duty, event, basic assumption and risk bearer.
- Distinguish impossible performance from frustrated purpose.
- Read the clause's remedy as carefully as its triggering event.
- Analyze prior benefits and earlier breaches separately from future-duty excuse.

lessons.title: Identify who may enforce a promised benefit
lessons.body:
A contract can benefit someone who never signed it. A parent purchases a child's lessons, an owner hires a builder whose work helps neighboring businesses, and a debtor arranges payment to a creditor. The third party's practical benefit does not answer whether that person may enforce the agreement. This lesson separates the existence of a benefit from an intended right and then examines the limits of that right.

Apply T1–T2 in the third-party reference. They are expressly selected teaching rules. Actual jurisdictions differ in how they express intent, recognize vesting and treat public contracts. We are not treating every person named in a contract as an enforceable beneficiary. The analysis begins with the promised performance and the relationship among the three people.

## Map the original promise

The **[[promisor]]** owes the particular promised performance. The **[[promisee]]** receives that promise in the original agreement. A **[[third-party beneficiary]]** is someone outside that original exchange who benefits from the promise. In a reciprocal contract, each party can be promisor for one obligation and promisee for another, so name the particular duty rather than permanently labeling one side “the promisor.”

An **[[intended beneficiary]]** has an enforceable benefit under T1 when recognition of enforcement fits the parties' manifested intention and the promise either satisfies the promisee's payment obligation to that person or is intended to confer the promised benefit on that person. An **[[incidental beneficiary]]** merely gains from the transaction without meeting that test. The word “incidental” describes legal status, not the financial size of the gain.

Look at terms, context and purpose. A clause directing a scholarship payment to a named student strongly supports intended benefit. A renovation contract that increases the neighboring cafe's sales ordinarily supplies only an incidental benefit under T1. The cafe may depend economically on the project, but dependence alone does not show that the contracting parties undertook a duty enforceable by the cafe.

## Intent is not just a name check

Being named can be evidence of intended benefit, yet the name may serve only to identify a destination or factual background. Conversely, T1 does not require every beneficiary to be identified by personal name at formation if the described class and circumstances sufficiently identify the intended recipient. Ask why the person or class appears in the agreement.

An **[[enforcement limitation]]** expressly reserves contractual enforcement to the original parties. Under T1, an applicable clear limitation ordinarily weighs against the claimed third-party right. Read its scope before treating it as conclusive: the limitation might govern only one promise or exclude one category. Mandatory rules outside the exercise could change the result, but do not invent such rules to evade the stated facts.

Separate public benefits from contractual enforcement. Many public projects help a broad population; that alone does not promise each resident an individual damages action. Our questions expressly exclude independent statutory claims. A beneficiary analysis therefore neither establishes nor defeats every possible noncontractual claim the person might have.

## Vesting constrains later changes

**[[Vesting]]** describes the point at which the original parties lose their ordinary power to change the beneficiary's right without consent under T2. The selected rule protects a beneficiary who, before receiving notice of modification, materially and justifiably relies, brings suit, or manifests requested assent to the promisor or promisee. A contract can reserve an applicable power of change, and the exercise states when it does.

This is a timing question. Identify the original promise, any reserved power, the beneficiary's qualifying act, and notice of the attempted change. Awareness alone is not the same as material reliance. Planning privately to spend a payment later is different from making a justified irreversible commitment because of the promised payment.

An unvested right can still be a right under T1. “Not yet vested” does not mean “always incidental.” Vesting concerns the original parties' power to alter an intended benefit. The distinction matters when a beneficiary sues before a purported modification or relies before learning of it.

## The beneficiary takes a bounded promise

Under T2, a beneficiary generally faces defenses and conditions arising from the promise it seeks to enforce. If payment was conditioned on a valid inspection and the condition remains unexcused, third-party status does not make the payment unconditional. If the promise is subject to a supported formation defense, the beneficiary cannot simply enlarge it into a new bargain.

Avoid **[[double recovery]]**, compensation twice for the same injury. The original promisee and intended beneficiary may have related enforcement interests, but their claims do not automatically multiply the amount owed. Distinct losses require distinct support. The exercise rule treats a proper payment as satisfying the same payment obligation once.

### Example 1: A creditor paid through another agreement

Nora owes Lee 3,000 dollars. Nora sells equipment to Vale for that price, and the written agreement directs Vale to pay Lee to discharge Nora's debt. There is no contrary enforcement term. Vale receives the equipment but refuses payment.

Map the promise: Vale promises payment; Nora receives that promise; Lee is outside the equipment exchange. The directed payment satisfies Nora's identified debt to Lee. Recognizing Lee's enforcement fits the manifested arrangement, so T1 supports intended-beneficiary status. Lee's claim is for the promised 3,000 dollars, not another 3,000 dollars on top of payment already made on that same obligation.

### Example 2: A change after justified reliance

A foundation contracts with a training provider to pay a named student's 2,000-dollar tuition. The agreement grants the student the benefit and reserves no modification power. The student receives the promise, reasonably and irreversibly pays 600 dollars for required travel in reliance, and only afterward receives notice that the foundation and provider want to substitute a different student.

T1 identifies an intended benefit. Under T2 the student's material, justified reliance before notice restricts modification without consent. The parties cannot disregard that timing by calling the change a private arrangement. If the student had merely heard a rumor and made no qualifying act, the vesting analysis would change. This example does not automatically award travel damages; it establishes the restriction on changing the promised tuition benefit.

## A writing exercise

Take a fictional contract for installing lighting in a shared courtyard. The text says only that the owner will pay the installer for safe lighting. A nearby shop expects increased evening sales. Write one paragraph identifying the shop's strongest intended-benefit argument and the stronger response under T1. Then add a clause expressly granting the shop a right to enforce the lighting promise. Explain why that is a relevant changed fact.

For each version, identify a defense that could survive beneficiary status. Use a condition already in the contract, not an invented unrelated grievance. This practice shows why establishing who may sue is only one step toward establishing what that person can recover.

## Primary reading

Compare [DeLine v CitiCapital Commercial Corp., 2005 NY Slip Op 09995](https://www.nycourts.gov/Reporter/3dseries/2005/2005_09995.htm) and [Logan-Baldwin v L.S.M. General Contractors, Inc., 2012 NY Slip Op 03046](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2012/2012_03046.htm). Both are New York intermediate appellate decisions. Identify how contract purpose and the available record affect the analysis; do not treat either as requiring a universal magic phrase.

## Common mistakes

- Equating a large economic benefit with an intended enforcement right.
- Treating any named person as automatically entitled to sue.
- Confusing the existence of an intended benefit with limits on later modification.
- Giving a beneficiary a promise free of its original conditions and defenses.

## Key points

- Map the particular promisor, promisee and third party.
- Identify manifested intention and the benefit the promise actually confers.
- Put reliance, assent, suit and modification notice on a timeline.
- Preserve applicable defenses and avoid duplicate satisfaction of one obligation.

lessons.title: Distinguish assignment, delegation and release
lessons.body:
Businesses transfer payment rights and use others to perform work. Those arrangements can look similar on a diagram while having different consequences. Transferring the right to receive money does not necessarily transfer the duty to provide services. Asking a subcontractor to do work does not necessarily release the original contractor. This lesson identifies exactly what moves and who remains responsible afterward.

T3–T4 govern these exercises. We examine ordinary contractual rights and performance, not secured-transactions priority, negotiable instruments, consumer-protection exceptions or bankruptcy. Those topics can alter real-world results. The selected rules and simplified facts keep the present focus on the distinction between rights, duties and release.

## Assignment transfers a right

An **[[assignment]]** transfers a contractual right from an **[[assignor]]** to an **[[assignee]]**. The person who owes the underlying performance is the **[[obligor]]**. If Sera earns a 5,000-dollar fee from a museum and assigns the receivable to a lender, Sera is assignor, the lender is assignee, and the museum is obligor on the payment duty.

Under T3, ordinary payment rights are assignable unless an applicable rule or effective restriction prevents transfer. Assignment is restricted when it would materially change the obligor's duty or materially increase its burden or risk. Transferring the destination of an unchanged payment is different from forcing an illustrator to provide a personal portrait for a new subject.

An **[[anti-assignment clause]]** requires interpretation. Its wording and the governing law determine whether it prohibits an act, makes a transfer ineffective, or leaves an accrued payment right transferable. T3's questions state the effect of any clause rather than assuming one phrase always produces one result. The New York goods reading also draws distinctions concerning earned rights and assignments of “the contract.”

## Identify defenses and notice

Under T3, the assignee ordinarily takes the assigned claim subject to the underlying contract's applicable defenses. If the assignor earned only 4,500 dollars after a stipulated 500-dollar defect adjustment, assignment of the receivable does not turn it into an unconditional 5,000-dollar claim. A new creditor is not automatically a better substantive creditor.

**[[Notice of assignment]]** informs the obligor that the right has moved. For our ordinary-payment exercises, payment to the assignor before effective notice discharges the payment obligation; after effective notice the obligor ordinarily must pay the assignee. The questions assume the assignment is valid and notice is adequate, and exclude priority disputes or statutory proof-request issues.

Distinguish notice from consent. An ordinary assignment may be valid without the obligor's permission under T3, while notice changes whom it can safely pay. Where a special duty materially depends on the recipient's identity, the transfer itself may require different analysis. Do not use the ordinary-payment example to decide a personal-services transfer.

## Delegation concerns performance

A **[[delegation]]** authorizes another person to perform a duty. The **[[delegator]]** is the original obligor on that duty; the **[[delegate]]** undertakes the work. T4 permits ordinary delegation unless the agreement bars it or the other party has a substantial interest in the original promisor's personal skill, judgment or control.

An ordinary cleaning company may be able to use qualified staff to supply the promised cleaning. A commission expressly for a named artist's distinctive performance presents a different interest. Ask what the recipient bought. A substitute can be equally capable in a general sense yet fail to supply the personal performance the agreement specifically sought.

Delegation alone does not release the original obligor under T4. If a permitted subcontractor fails, the original contractor remains responsible for its promise. The fact that the recipient accepted some work from the substitute is not necessarily an agreement to surrender recourse against the original party.

An **[[assumption of duty]]** occurs when the delegate promises to perform the delegated obligation. It may create enforceable obligations under the applicable rule, but it does not itself erase the delegator's liability. Identify the delegate's promise separately from the original promise. A bare assignment of payment rights need not include either delegation or assumption.

## Novation requires an actual substitution agreement

A **[[novation]]** substitutes an obligation or obligor through an agreement that extinguishes the former duty. For our party-substitution problems, T4 requires the necessary parties' assent to the substitution and release. A **[[release]]** gives up the identified claim or obligation; it is not inferred merely from knowing a subcontractor is present.

Use clear language in your analysis: “The owner accepted performance by the substitute” describes conduct. “The owner agreed to release the original builder and look solely to the substitute” describes the additional fact needed by our novation rule. Do not supply the second sentence unless the record supports it.

### Example 1: Payment after notice

Arun earns a 7,000-dollar design fee, subject to an agreed 500-dollar correction offset. Arun validly assigns the receivable to Finch Finance. The customer receives effective notice before making payment, but later pays Arun anyway. All parties agree that T3's ordinary-payment rule governs.

The assigned enforceable balance is 6,500 dollars, not 7,000, because the underlying correction defense remains. Effective notice directed payment to Finch. Payment to Arun afterward does not discharge the assigned obligation under T3. The customer may have a separate claim against Arun, but that does not automatically satisfy Finch's right. Changing the payment date to before effective notice changes the discharge analysis.

### Example 2: A substitute crew without release

A community center hires North Crew for ordinary cleaning. Delegation to qualified staff is permitted. North Crew hires West Crew, which promises to do the work but fails. The center knew West Crew would perform; it never agreed to release North Crew.

T4 permits the delegation, so using West Crew is not itself a breach. The failure to supply cleaning is the breach. North Crew remains responsible because delegation did not extinguish its promise. West Crew's assumption may also create an enforceable duty under the stipulated arrangement, but the center cannot recover twice for the same cleaning loss. A three-party agreement expressly substituting West Crew and releasing North Crew would raise novation instead.

## Practice mapping without losing the duty

Draw a table with one row for each promise and columns for original obligor, original right holder, assignee, delegate and release. Leave inapplicable cells blank. This is more reliable than drawing a single arrow labeled “contract transferred,” which conceals whether rights, duties or both changed.

Then test a personal-service variation: a famous muralist assigns a right to receive an already earned fee and separately proposes that an unknown artist paint the remaining commissioned mural. Explain why the payment assignment and performance delegation require different analyses even though they arise from one agreement.

## Primary reading

Read [New York UCC § 2-210](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/UCC/2-210). Locate its distinction between assignment and delegation, its material-change limits, its treatment of earned rights, and its statement that delegation does not relieve the delegating party. The provision governs its goods context and refers to Article 9; it does not resolve every service receivable or priority question.

## Common mistakes

- Describing every transfer as an assignment without identifying what moved.
- Assuming an assignee escapes the underlying contract's defenses.
- Treating permission to delegate as permission to abandon responsibility.
- Inferring novation from mere knowledge of substitute performance.

## Key points

- Assignment moves a right; delegation concerns a duty's performance.
- Notice affects payment discharge under the stated ordinary-payment rule.
- Personal performance interests and restrictions can limit transfers.
- A release of the original obligor requires additional support.

lessons.title: Compare monetary remedies without counting a loss twice
lessons.body:
Finding a breach does not produce a damages number by itself. You must identify whose position is being restored, select a measure, connect each claimed loss to the breach and apply limits. A receipt proves money changed hands; it does not necessarily prove that the entire amount is recoverable in addition to every other claim. This lesson makes the comparison explicit.

Apply R1–R4 in the remedies reference. Monetary figures are in dollars, and the questions specify when a loss is proven, foreseeable, reasonable or avoidable. Those stipulations let you practice the calculation. In real litigation each label would require evidence and a governing rule. The capstone will ask you to distinguish stipulated facts from contested assertions.

## Begin with the promised position

The **[[expectation interest]]** aims to place the injured party in the position performance would have produced, subject to limits. R1 expresses the basic comparison as loss in value plus other recoverable loss minus costs or losses avoided. It is not a guarantee of the claimant's most optimistic imagined outcome.

For an owner purchasing replacement services after the contractor abandons the whole job without supplying value, use total reasonable completion outlay minus the original agreed price, with supported additional losses and savings. Total outlay includes an unreturned advance paid to the original contractor. If you instead subtract the unpaid original balance from substitute cost, you have already accounted for that advance. Do not add it again.

For a performing seller whose buyer breaches, distinguish the unpaid revenue from costs the seller no longer needs to incur. Expected net profit plus unreimbursed performance costs can express the same comparison in an appropriately stated problem. Lost-volume, resale and market-price problems may require additional rules; we do not decide them from a generic subtraction.

**[[Incidental damages]]** cover reasonable expenses associated with responding to breach under the applicable rule. **[[Consequential damages]]** concern additional losses arising from the claimant's circumstances. The classification alone does not establish recoverability. A reasonable substitute-search fee differs from projected event income, but both require the relevant causal and limiting analysis.

## Apply the limits to each item

**[[Causation]]** asks whether the breach produced the claimed loss. A roof damaged by an unrelated storm is not charged to a late consultant simply because the events occurred in the same week. Identify the mechanism, not merely the sequence.

**[[Foreseeability]]** under R2 asks whether the type of loss was foreseeable at contract formation as an ordinary result or because relevant special circumstances were known. A previously undisclosed collateral venture may fail this requirement. Later notice after breach does not retroactively establish what the parties knew when making the agreement.

**[[Reasonable certainty]]** requires a supported basis for the amount; it does not require mathematical perfection. Historical sales, actual bookings and itemized costs can support a claim more strongly than an unexplained optimistic estimate. **[[Net profit]]** subtracts expenses required to generate revenue. Claiming gross ticket sales while ignoring avoided catering costs exaggerates the performance position.

**[[Mitigation]]** limits recovery for harm reasonably avoidable without undue risk or burden. Under R2, evaluate the response using the circumstances then known. Reasonable unsuccessful efforts can be recoverable; hindsight does not make them foolish automatically. **[[Avoided costs]]** are expenses the breach saves. Deduct a saving only once, and verify it is not already included in a stated net-profit figure.

## Compare reliance and restitution

The **[[reliance interest]]** concerns reasonable expenditure caused by entering or preparing to perform the agreement. R3 permits that measure when applicable, subject to proof and subtraction of any losing-bargain amount the breaching party establishes. It cannot simply guarantee a profitless bargain against a proven loss that performance itself would have caused.

The **[[restitution interest]]** concerns a benefit conferred on the other party, rather than every cost the claimant incurred. Under R4, an injured party after the specified total breach may seek return of an advance or the reasonable value of a recoverable benefit, subject to offsets and eligibility limits. Money paid to an unrelated printer is a possible reliance expenditure; it is not automatically a benefit retained by the breaching contractor.

**[[Quantum meruit]]** is a reasonable-value theory often associated with services and restitution, but it is not a universal way to rewrite an enforceable price. R4 expressly excludes the fully performed fixed-price situation in which only payment remains due from its alternative restitution exercise. Applicable law and contract status matter.

### Example 1: Replacement and savings

A hall buys installation services for 20,000 dollars and pays a 4,000-dollar advance. The contractor repudiates before doing any work and keeps the advance. A reasonable identical substitute costs 23,000 dollars. An additional 600-dollar emergency coordination fee is recoverable, and the breach saves a separate 200-dollar storage expense.

Total completion outlay is 4,000 plus 23,000, or 27,000 dollars. Subtract the original 20,000-dollar price to obtain 7,000. Add 600 and subtract 200: expectation damages are 7,400 dollars. Equivalently, subtract the unpaid original balance of 16,000 from the substitute cost of 23,000, then add 400 net other loss. Both routes produce 7,400. Adding the advance again to that result would duplicate it.

### Example 2: Two alternative interests

A buyer spends 5,000 dollars reasonably preparing for performance, including a 2,000-dollar advance to the breaching seller and 3,000 paid to others. No value is returned. For this separate problem, the seller proves that full performance would have caused the buyer a 1,000-dollar net loss. R3's reliance measure is therefore 4,000 dollars, assuming all stated expenditures qualify.

R4's simple advance-return alternative is 2,000 dollars because only that amount benefited the seller, and no offset is supplied. The alternatives answer different questions. You cannot add 4,000 reliance to 2,000 restitution when the same advance is already within the reliance expenditure. Nor can you call all 5,000 a benefit retained by the seller.

## Prepare an auditable schedule

Use columns for item, evidence, measure, amount, limitation and overlap. Write a short sentence explaining each deduction. If a question provides net event profit, ask which costs were already subtracted before taking another saving. If the facts state only revenue, request costs rather than pretending the revenue equals damages.

For a goods comparison, **[[cover]]** is a reasonable substitute purchase under the selected sales rule. The measure compares cover cost with the contract price, adds qualifying incidental and consequential losses and subtracts savings. Failure to cover does not automatically eliminate every other remedy, although avoidable consequential losses may remain unrecoverable.

## Primary reading

Compare [New York UCC § 2-712](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/UCC/2-712) and [§ 2-715](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/UCC/2-715). Identify the substitute-purchase requirements and the separate limits on additional loss. These goods provisions illustrate why the formula and its qualifying conditions must travel together. R1–R4 expressly supply the services and alternative-interest assumptions used here.

The same litigation later returned to the [Appellate Division in 2014](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2014/2014_07035.htm). After remand, proof that the project was infeasible supported limiting recovery of preparation expenses; the appellate court adjusted interest. Compare recognition of an available reliance claim in 2009 with proof of recoverable loss afterward. Reinstating a claim does not promise recovery of every expenditure.

## Common mistakes

- Adding an advance twice when the replacement calculation already includes it.
- Claiming gross revenue instead of supported net profit.
- Treating every expenditure as a benefit received by the defendant.
- Adding alternative measures that compensate the same loss.

## Key points

- State the protected interest before doing arithmetic.
- Test each claimed item for causation and applicable limits.
- Track savings, payments and overlapping components explicitly.
- Show alternative measures separately and explain why they differ.

lessons.title: Evaluate agreed and equitable relief, then write the breach memorandum
lessons.body:
Money is the usual starting point for contract relief, but some disputes involve a unique subject or a pre-agreed damages term. This final lesson compares those possibilities and then brings the course together in a complete fictional file. Your task is a reasoned memorandum with an auditable damages schedule. A large number or confident conclusion does not substitute for explaining the right, breach, defense and measure.

R5–R6 supply the selected rules for this lesson. The Cedar Hall record provides all facts for the capstone; its model and rubric are separate so you can attempt the work first. The writing assignment is self-assessed. Completing the app's objective quiz does not certify the quality of your memorandum or award university credit.

## Equitable relief asks why money is inadequate

**[[Specific performance]]** orders the promised performance when the applicable equitable requirements are met. Under R5, show why money would not adequately substitute, consider definiteness and feasibility, and address fairness. **[[Inadequacy of damages]]** is not established merely because the claimant prefers the original contractor. Ready availability of equivalent performance weakens the argument.

A genuinely unique identified object can support specific relief. The selected goods comparison allows specific performance for unique goods or other proper circumstances; uniqueness is not its only statutory phrase. An ordinary product with plentiful substitutes presents a different case. The inability to obtain an appropriate substitute may matter even where the item does not resemble a museum masterpiece.

An **[[injunction]]** directs or restrains conduct. It is not interchangeable with an award of damages. R5 does not authorize compelling personal services. A request that a named musician sing at a concert raises concerns distinct from delivery of an identified object. A negative restraint also requires its own legal and equitable analysis; do not assume that forbidding all other work is a permissible shortcut to forcing the promised performance.

Equitable relief also cannot duplicate compensation for the same promised benefit. A court may combine appropriate forms of relief for distinct losses under the applicable law, but the claimant must identify what each component does. Receiving the unique object and its full substitute value would ordinarily overcompensate under the course's no-duplication rule.

## Agreed damages still require scrutiny

**[[Liquidated damages]]** are an amount or formula fixed in advance for breach. Under R6, the selected inquiry examines reasonableness in light of anticipated or actual harm and difficulty of proof. A **[[penalty]]** is an unreasonably large amount used to punish rather than reasonably compensate under that rule. Calling a clause “liquidated damages” does not establish validity.

For illustration, a commercially supported daily delay estimate can be reasonable where loss is hard to measure, while a huge fixed payment for any trivial defect may be disproportionate. Avoid deciding by amount alone. Compare the trigger, possible range of harm and evidentiary basis. Our selected rule follows the identified goods provision's phrasing; common-law tests and consumer contexts can differ.

A **[[remedy limitation]]** can restrict available relief, such as an exclusive repair remedy. That raises questions beyond whether a damages number is a penalty. The later Sales course addresses failure of essential purpose and related provisions in greater detail. Here, do not infer a valid limitation from a clause that the record does not contain.

### Example 1: An identified unique object

A seller agrees to sell an identified original sculpture and then refuses delivery. The buyer cannot obtain an equivalent substitute, the object still exists in the seller's possession, and the agreement is definite. No fairness or feasibility obstacle is supplied.

Under R5, the uniqueness and lack of an adequate substitute support a request for specific performance. The conclusion is a supported argument for equitable relief, not a declaration that every unique object automatically produces an order. Change the facts to an ordinary chair available from several sellers at an ascertainable price, and monetary substitution becomes the stronger starting point.

### Example 2: A stated sum disconnected from harm

A routine goods contract fixes 50,000 dollars for any delivery defect. The defect is a one-hour delay causing 20 dollars of readily measured loss, and the parties reasonably anticipated similarly small losses when agreeing. There is no other relevant anticipated or actual harm.

Under R6, the fixed sum is unreasonably large relative to both anticipated and actual harm and has no stated proof-difficulty justification. The facts support treating it as a penalty rather than valid liquidated damages. That does not mean the injured party receives nothing; supported ordinary damages remain a separate question.

## Cedar Hall assignment

Read the complete record R01–R12 in the Cedar Hall reference. Assume a valid services agreement and apply the numbered exercise rules, not an invented Cedar jurisdiction. Write 900–1,200 words addressed to a supervising study partner, plus a separate calculation table. Allocate roughly twenty minutes to the record, sixty to drafting, twenty to checking the model and twenty to revision.

Your memorandum should identify the performance and payment conditions, classify the contractor's October 10 message, analyze the attempted October 13 retraction, and evaluate the stated excuse and delegation arguments. Explain why the named community group and the neighboring cafe occupy different positions. Distinguish the lender's assigned payment right from a right to payment that has actually matured.

For relief, calculate Cedar Hall's expectation claim under the record's stipulated components, show the advance-return alternative, and explain overlap. Evaluate specific performance and the unsupported demand for punitive recovery. State which loss component remains evidentially contested even though its arithmetic is supplied for the assumed calculation.

The capstone's date sequence is part of its reasoning. Do not infer that the original contractor may retract just because the ultimate performance date has not arrived. The replacement agreement intervenes. Equally, do not assume hiring a delegate releases the original contractor when the record expressly denies a release.

## Review and revise

After drafting, open the separate model. Mark every sentence in your memorandum as rule, fact, application or conclusion. If an application paragraph contains only rules, add the specific record facts that support or weaken the outcome. If you state a disputed fact as proven, qualify the prediction and identify the evidence needed.

Use the 24-point rubric as a revision aid, not an automated score. Record one correction to the damages table and one strengthened counterargument. Then answer the changed-fact questions without merely changing party names. A later replacement date, an actual agreed release, or a covered flood can change the analysis for different reasons.

## Primary reading

Compare [New York UCC § 2-716](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/UCC/2-716) and [§ 2-718(1)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/UCC/2-718). Identify the words that make the inquiry broader than “unique goods only” and the considerations used to evaluate agreed damages. These are enacted New York goods rules; R5–R6 expressly govern the fictional teaching exercises.

## Common mistakes

- Treating a preference for the original provider as proof money is inadequate.
- Enforcing a punitive sum because the contract labels it liquidated damages.
- Adding a deposit refund to an expectation calculation that already accounts for it.
- Treating quiz completion as substantive approval of a written memorandum.

## Key points

- Explain the inadequacy of money and the feasibility of requested equitable relief.
- Evaluate an agreed amount against the selected rule and actual facts.
- Trace rights, duties, dates and defenses before calculating relief.
- Revise the memorandum and calculation together so they tell the same story.

banks.title: Contracts II: Performance, Breach and Remedies questions

sections.name: Expectation, reliance, restitution and equitable relief

questions.stem: P1 governs. Payment is due only if an outside foundation awards a grant. Nobody promised to obtain the grant, and no excuse applies. The foundation declines. What follows?
choices: The contract fails at formation because the grant was part of the consideration.
The payment duty does not mature, without breach from the grant’s absence alone.
The applicant breaches an implied promise that the foundation will award the grant.
The payer owes the price, with the denied grant treated only as a damages offset.
questions.explanation: P1 separates a condition controlling payment from a promise to cause the event. Here the award is absent, no excuse applies, and nobody undertook to obtain it.

questions.stem: Under P1, which clause most clearly states an express condition of final payment?
choices: The contractor promises to request an inspection on Friday.
The contractor expects certification to be straightforward.
The parties will discuss inspection scheduling next week.
Final payment is due only if the specified safety certificate issues.
questions.explanation: The correct clause expressly links the payment duty to issuance. A commitment to request inspection is a promise, and expectations or planned discussion do not alone establish that condition.

questions.stem: P1 governs a simultaneous exchange. The seller tenders the promised item ready for transfer, but the buyer neither brings nor offers the agreed payment. Which analysis fits?
choices: The buyer has not supplied the tender needed to demand the concurrent exchange.
The seller must first complete delivery before the buyer must tender payment.
The buyer’s willingness to pay later is enough to satisfy the concurrent tender.
The seller’s withholding pending tender is itself a material failure to deliver.
questions.explanation: Under the stipulated concurrent-exchange rule, the buyer must make a ready and able tender. The seller's demand for the agreed simultaneous return is not itself repudiation.

questions.stem: A clause is genuinely ambiguous between a completion promise and an express payment condition. The latter reading creates forfeiture. What interpretive preference does P1 supply?
choices: Prefer the condition reading because payment and completion concern the same exchange.
Prefer the condition reading, but excuse its nonoccurrence whenever some work was done.
Prefer the promise reading and award the full price without any defect adjustment.
Prefer the promise reading while still enforcing supported breach consequences.
questions.explanation: P1's preference avoids construing doubtful language as an express condition causing forfeiture. It does not erase the promise or convert it into optional performance.

questions.stem: P2 governs. An owner owes timely inspection, refuses it solely to avoid paying, and thereby prevents the required certificate. What is the strongest response?
choices: The contractor must first show substantial performance to excuse the obstruction.
The owner cannot rely on the certificate’s absence its wrongful obstruction caused.
The certificate remains essential because the inspector did not issue it in writing.
The obstruction changes only the due date; it cannot affect the certificate condition.
questions.explanation: Prevention requires wrongful interference and causation. Both are supplied, so the owner cannot use its own obstruction to defeat the controlled duty; punitive relief does not follow automatically.

questions.stem: A condition protects only the buyer. The buyer clearly waives it; the seller then materially and justifiably relies. Under P2, may the buyer suddenly insist on it without honoring that reliance?
choices: Yes; the original written condition controls over the later statement of waiver.
Yes; withdrawal before the payment date is enough despite the seller’s reliance.
No; the stipulated waiver rule prevents restoration after that reliance.
No; the initial waiver is irrevocable even without reliance or any other limit.
questions.explanation: P2 allows waiver of the buyer's own protection and limits reinstatement after material justified reliance. The waiver concerns the identified condition, not every contractual duty.

questions.stem: Under P2, why is disproportionate forfeiture alone insufficient to excuse a genuine safety approval central to the bargain?
choices: The excuse also requires that the event not be a material part of the exchange.
The excuse requires a failure caused by the payer, even when forfeiture is severe.
The excuse applies only to implied conditions and never to an express condition.
The excuse requires measuring forfeiture solely against the cost of the certificate.
questions.explanation: P2 does not erase a material safety condition merely because compliance or nonpayment is harsh. Materiality of the event remains a distinct limit.

questions.stem: A payer declines an inspection appointment outside the agreed inspection period. The record states no duty to attend then. What is missing from a P2 prevention argument?
choices: A showing that the contractor would suffer a large loss without the final payment.
A showing that the certificate affects payment rather than contract formation.
A basis for treating that refusal as wrongful interference with required cooperation.
A showing that the payer could physically have attended the proposed appointment.
questions.explanation: Prevention is not established by any obstacle or refusal. The analyst must identify required cooperation and wrongful conduct that caused nonoccurrence.

questions.stem: Match each description to its term in the conditions framework.
left: Ready and able offer of the agreed exchange
choices: Promise
Condition
Tender
questions.explanation: Commitment to submit plans — Promise; Uncertain approval controlling payment — Condition; Ready and able offer of the agreed exchange — Tender. These roles or concepts must remain distinct in analysis.

questions.stem: Under P2, intentionally relinquishing a condition's protection is called ___.
questions.explanation: Waiver concerns intentional relinquishment of the identified protection; it does not automatically release every duty.

questions.stem: Under P3, which fact most strongly supports materiality of an unfinished installation?
choices: A missing safety feature makes the installation unusable for its agreed purpose.
One replaceable handle has a small cosmetic scratch.
The provider completed fewer administrative tasks than anticipated.
The owner now dislikes the price despite receiving safe usable work.
questions.explanation: Materiality concerns deprivation of the promised benefit, not task counting or regret. An unusable unsafe installation directly undermines the exchange.

questions.stem: P3 applies. A 10,000-dollar service job is substantially performed; 100 dollars is the stipulated proper defect offset. No other adjustment applies. What is due?
choices: 10,000 dollars.
9,900 dollars.
100 dollars.
0 dollars.
questions.explanation: Substantial performance permits the due price subject to defect damages: 10,000 minus 100 equals 9,900. It neither forgives defects nor grants free performance.

questions.stem: P3 permits suspension while a material failure remains uncured. Which conclusion requires additional support?
choices: That the failure may justify temporarily withholding dependent performance.
That cure prospects can affect the next response.
That the significance of delay should be evaluated.
That remaining duties are permanently discharged by a total breach.
questions.explanation: Suspension and discharge differ. P3 requires facts supporting total breach before treating remaining duties as permanently ended.

questions.stem: A contractor offers prompt, reliable repair of an accidental minor defect in an otherwise usable project. No express condition applies. Under P3, why does the offer matter?
choices: Offering repair means the owner has no claim for losses already caused by the defect.
The repair offer requires treating the defective work as conforming tender at delivery.
Likely cure bears on whether ending remaining performance is justified.
The owner may disregard cure because materiality is fixed solely at initial delivery.
questions.explanation: Cure likelihood is a materiality and response consideration. It does not automatically erase loss or justify delay past an essential use date.

questions.stem: P4 governs a single-delivery goods contract before acceptance. Red folders arrive instead of the promised blue ones. What is the starting rule?
choices: The buyer must accept usable folders and seek only the difference in their value.
The buyer must first allow a reasonable repair period before giving rejection notice.
Timely rejection ends the seller’s right to cure even while contract time remains.
Timely rejection with notice is available, subject to the agreement and cure rules.
questions.explanation: P4 uses a nonconforming-tender starting point while preserving timely notice and cure. It is not the services substantial-performance rule.

questions.stem: Delivery is due Friday. Nonconforming goods are timely rejected Tuesday; the seller seasonably gives cure notice and delivers conforming goods Thursday. P4 applies. What follows?
choices: The seller also needs reasonable grounds for believing Tuesday’s tender acceptable.
The seller has used the within-contract-time cure route.
The buyer must separately agree to a new delivery date for Thursday’s cure to count.
The cure fails because the buyer exercised rejection before the seller sent notice.
questions.explanation: Contract time remained, notice was timely, and conforming delivery occurred before Friday. The initial defect alone does not negate this effective cure.

questions.stem: Goods were already accepted. The buyer later discovers a serious defect. What does this course's P4 caution require?
