choices: Limit the buyer to the price difference because acceptance precludes any return remedy.
Apply substantial performance because acceptance converts goods into a services dispute.
Analyze revocation or accepted-goods remedies instead of simply reusing initial rejection.
Apply initial rejection requirements because the defect was discovered after acceptance.
questions.explanation: Acceptance changes the remedial framework. Revocation has separate requirements; neither unlimited rejection nor universal loss of remedy follows.

questions.stem: Contract time has expired after a rejected tender. Under P4, what could support the separate further-reasonable-time cure route?
choices: Reasonable grounds to believe the original tender acceptable, plus seasonable cure notice.
Ability to deliver conforming goods soon, without grounds for the earlier tender’s acceptance.
Seasonable notice alone, with the remaining requirements measured as if the deadline had not passed.
A tender worth most of the price, without regard to reasonable belief or cure notice.
questions.explanation: P4 identifies reasonable belief and seasonable notice for the additional cure route. Expiration does not itself establish either automatic cure or automatic defeat.

questions.stem: Match each description to its term in the material breach framework.
left: Temporary withholding while a serious failure remains
Enough performance to trigger return duty with defect damages
Correcting a deficient tender under the applicable rule
choices: Suspension
Substantial performance
Cure
questions.explanation: Temporary withholding while a serious failure remains — Suspension; Enough performance to trigger return duty with defect damages — Substantial performance; Correcting a deficient tender under the applicable rule — Cure. These roles or concepts must remain distinct in analysis.

questions.stem: P4 calls the initial single-delivery conformity starting point the ___ rule.
questions.explanation: Perfect tender is a starting rule bounded by acceptance status, notice, contract terms and cure.

questions.stem: B1 applies. Which message most clearly repudiates the agreed material performance?
choices: I am checking a staffing problem but still expect to deliver as agreed.
Could we discuss whether you want an optional extra feature?
Our driver changed, and the confirmed replacement will deliver on time.
I will not deliver at the agreed price, now or on the due date.
questions.explanation: The correct message unequivocally refuses the existing bargain. Concern, optional discussion and confirmed substitute performance do not communicate the same refusal.

questions.stem: A material performance is repudiated May 1. A reasonable binding substitute is obtained May 3. Retraction arrives May 4 before the original due date. Under B1, which fact blocks reinstatement?
choices: The repudiation itself, even without any intervening response by the injured party.
The fact that the repudiation and retraction occurred on different calendar dates.
The injured party materially changed position before the retraction.
The failure to wait until the original performance date before securing a replacement.
questions.explanation: The binding reasonable replacement is the stipulated material change. The performance date alone does not preserve retraction against that intervening response.

questions.stem: A party says it can return only for 8,000 dollars more than the agreed price. Why is this not necessarily an effective B1 retraction?
choices: It does not clearly restore willingness to perform the original obligation.
Any proposed price change automatically discharges the existing agreement.
Retraction requires acceptance by the injured party even absent an intervening barrier.
The original refusal becomes a present breach only when the due date arrives.
questions.explanation: Retraction concerns the existing obligation. A conditional return at a higher price can continue the refusal of that bargain.

questions.stem: A party chooses to wait after a qualifying repudiation. Under B1, how should later damages be evaluated?
choices: Losses remain recoverable until the due date without regard to an available substitute.
Choosing to wait prevents recovery for losses caused by the earlier repudiation.
Waiting is unreasonable whenever a substitute exists, regardless of the circumstances.
Waiting must remain reasonable and avoidable losses remain subject to mitigation.
questions.explanation: The rule permits a reasonable wait, not unlimited accumulation of avoidable loss or an automatic permanent surrender of remedies.

questions.stem: B2 applies to goods. Verified closure of the seller's only plant jeopardizes delivery. What response fits the selected rule?
choices: A final cancellation based solely on the closure, without assessing substitute capacity.
A written demand for adequate assurance of due performance.
An oral assurance demand treated as satisfying B2’s stated written-demand requirement.
A demand for a price reduction as assurance, even if reliable production can be shown.
questions.explanation: Verified closure can supply reasonable grounds. B2's procedure seeks assurance of the existing bargain through a written demand, not a new economic advantage.

questions.stem: Under B2, what does the thirty-day assurance limit mean?
choices: Assurance is due in a reasonable time that cannot exceed thirty days.
The recipient has thirty days even when the circumstances justify a shorter response time.
The thirty days begins on the delivery date even if the justified demand arrived earlier.
The demander must specify thirty days for its demand to be effective under the rule.
questions.explanation: Thirty days is the ceiling, not a mandatory grace period. Circumstances may make a shorter response time reasonable.

questions.stem: A merchant seller promptly supplies assurance stipulated adequate under trade standards. What happens to a suspension based solely on the resolved insecurity under B2?
choices: The suspension continues until thirty days have run despite the adequate response.
The suspension continues until completed delivery even after adequate assurance arrives.
That justified suspension ends when adequate assurance resolves the insecurity.
The suspension becomes cancellation because the initial grounds were reasonable.
questions.explanation: Adequate assurance addresses the grounds for the temporary suspension. B2 does not convert it into leverage for unrelated changes.

questions.stem: A services customer invokes the goods statute's assurance procedure, but no services assurance rule or contractual right is supplied. What is the best analysis?
choices: Apply B2 to services by analogy without identifying a rule authorizing the procedure.
Identify an applicable services or contract rule before assuming the goods procedure governs.
Deny any assurance right because service parties cannot agree to an assurance procedure.
Use B1 to treat the absence of assurance as repudiation without a qualifying refusal.
questions.explanation: The course deliberately limits B2 to its goods comparison. A services assurance right must come from a stated applicable rule, not silent transplantation.

questions.stem: Match each description to its term in the repudiation framework.
left: Clear refusal of material future performance
Clear withdrawal subject to intervening limits
choices: Repudiation
Retraction
Adequate assurance
questions.explanation: Clear refusal of material future performance — Repudiation; Clear withdrawal subject to intervening limits — Retraction; Evidence resolving justified future-performance concern — Adequate assurance. These roles or concepts must remain distinct in analysis.

questions.stem: Under B2, a justified demand seeks adequate ___ of due performance.
questions.explanation: The demanded assurance must be adequate under the circumstances; the procedure does not authorize a replacement bargain.

questions.stem: Under B3, ordinary paper prices rise within normal market variation in a fixed-price folder contract. Equivalent supplies remain available. What is the strongest analysis?
choices: The reduced margin establishes impracticability even within ordinary market fluctuation.
The ordinary allocated cost risk does not establish excuse on those facts.
The price increase frustrates the seller’s principal purpose because profit was expected.
The fixed price entitles the seller to an adjustment for increased input costs.
questions.explanation: B3 distinguishes ordinary market risk from a qualifying extraordinary event. The supplied facts preserve availability and allocate normal cost variation.

questions.stem: Both parties identify viewing a unique procession as the sole purpose of a balcony rental. It is permanently cancelled without fault or allocated risk; the balcony remains usable. Which B3 doctrine fits best?
choices: Objective impossibility of supplying the usable balcony.
Frustration of purpose.
Commercial impracticability caused by an increased cost of supplying the balcony.
Failure of an express cancellation condition that neither party actually included.
questions.explanation: Performance remains physically possible, while the mutually recognized principal purpose is destroyed. That identifies frustration under the stipulated facts.

questions.stem: An undisclosed private hope becomes impossible, but the contract's mutually recognized purpose remains intact. What weakens a B3 frustration claim?
choices: The defeated motive was not the shared principal purpose of the exchange.
The disappointment occurred after formation rather than before the bargain was made.
The party could still pay, so destruction of a principal purpose could not matter.
The contract omitted a force majeure clause, so frustration could not apply.
questions.explanation: B3 requires a principal purpose recognized by both parties, not an uncommunicated hope the other party never undertook to support.

questions.stem: A short qualifying closure ends, and later performance would still supply materially the same exchange. Under B3, which consequence should be considered?
choices: Temporary suspension rather than automatic permanent discharge.
Permanent discharge because performance was impossible on at least one day.
Breach damages for every day of delay despite the stipulated qualifying excuse.
An indefinite extension without considering when the obstacle ceased.
questions.explanation: The duration and bargain's purpose determine whether delay suffices. A temporary obstacle does not automatically justify permanent discharge or erase prior breach.

questions.stem: B4's clause covers official flood closure and excludes ordinary staffing changes. Alder moves workers to a more profitable job; no flood occurs. What follows?
choices: The clause covers the labor shortage because it delays the agreed installation.
The clause extends to business events similar in effect to the named flood closure.
The clause gives an extension if Alder provides notice of its staffing decision.
The supplied event does not trigger the clause.
questions.explanation: The actual trigger and exclusion control. A voluntary staffing choice is not the specified official flood closure.

questions.stem: A covered closure triggers a clause granting an extension equal to the closure period after prompt notice. Notice is satisfied. What relief does B4 support?
choices: Discharge of the remaining exchange instead of the specified delay remedy.
An extension lasting until the affected party finds performance commercially attractive.
An extension beginning when notice was sent rather than measured by closure duration.
The stated extension, subject to the clause’s terms.
questions.explanation: A covered event does not expand the clause's remedy. The agreement supplies an extension, not the other consequences.

questions.stem: A qualifying event reduces a goods seller's capacity by half. Under B3's selected goods rule, what further requirements matter?
choices: Allocation to the highest-price contracts, with notice only after capacity is restored.
Cancellation of all affected contracts, even when half the capacity remains available.
Fair, reasonable allocation and seasonable notice including the required estimated quota.
An equal-percentage allocation in every case, without the separate notice requirement.
questions.explanation: The partial-capacity rule requires fair and reasonable allocation plus notice. It is neither secret favoritism nor automatic universal cancellation.

questions.stem: A qualifying event excuses a future duty, but the party retains an advance for which no benefit was supplied. What must the analyst do?
choices: Treat the advance as earned because the future duty has been excused.
Treat excuse as rescission at formation and disregard any benefit actually conferred.
Analyze the retained benefit under a separate restitution rule.
Refund every payment immediately without evaluating counterbenefits or offsets.
questions.explanation: Excuse of future performance does not itself settle the treatment of prior benefits. Restitution eligibility and offsets require separate analysis.

questions.stem: Match each description to its term in the excuse framework.
left: Performance objectively cannot occur under the stated facts
Shared principal purpose is substantially destroyed
choices: Impossibility
Frustration of purpose
Allocated commercial risk
questions.explanation: Performance objectively cannot occur under the stated facts — Impossibility; Shared principal purpose is substantially destroyed — Frustration of purpose; Ordinary fixed-price market fluctuation — Allocated commercial risk. These roles or concepts must remain distinct in analysis.

questions.stem: A contract provision addressing specified disruptive events is a ___ clause.
questions.explanation: A force majeure clause must be read for trigger, causation, exclusions, notice and the relief actually promised.

questions.stem: Nora owes Lee 3,000 dollars and contracts for Vale to pay Lee in satisfaction of that debt. T1 applies and no contrary term exists. Which status best fits Lee?
choices: An incidental beneficiary merely because Lee did not sign.
An intended beneficiary of Vale's payment promise.
An assignee solely because Lee receives the promised money.
A delegate responsible for Vale's performance.
questions.explanation: The promised payment satisfies Nora's identified obligation to Lee and fits the manifested arrangement. No transfer or delegated duty is stated.

questions.stem: A cafe expects greater sales from nearby renovation. The contract grants it no intended benefit or enforcement right. Under T1, increased sales alone establish what?
choices: An intended enforcement right if the cafe can prove substantial lost sales.
An incidental economic benefit, not an enforceable intended benefit.
An intended enforcement right because renovation benefits nearby businesses foreseeably.
A vested contractual right when the cafe learns about the planned renovation.
questions.explanation: The size of an advantage does not establish contractual enforcement intent. Assignment and novation require different facts.

questions.stem: A person is named solely as a delivery landmark in a contract. Under T1, what does the name establish?
choices: Relevant context, but not by itself an intended right to enforce.
An intended benefit because identifying the person supplies the required intention.
A right to enforce the delivery promise once the person learns its name appears.
A payment right if the person can prove economic reliance on the delivery date.
questions.explanation: Naming can serve informational purposes. T1 asks what benefit and enforcement intention the promise manifests.

questions.stem: Under T1, why must the analyst identify the particular promise before labeling the promisor and promisee?
choices: The party owing the money is the promisor for every promise in the transaction.
The party arranging a third-party benefit is the promisor regardless of the duty at issue.
A reciprocal party can owe one performance while receiving another promise.
The beneficiary’s favored party must be the promisee of every reciprocal obligation.
questions.explanation: Roles attach to a particular obligation. Reciprocal promises can reverse the roles across different duties.

questions.stem: T2 applies without a reserved change power. Before notice of modification, an intended beneficiary materially and justifiably relies. What follows?
choices: The original parties’ power to change that benefit without consent is restricted.
The original parties retain unrestricted change power until the beneficiary files suit.
The beneficiary’s reliance removes every condition on the underlying performance.
The beneficiary must also give requested assent before reliance can restrict changes.
questions.explanation: Qualifying reliance before notice restricts modification of the intended benefit. It does not establish every remedy or freeze all terms regardless of consent.

questions.stem: A beneficiary merely learns of a promised payment and privately hopes to spend it, taking no qualifying act. What does T2 say about that knowledge alone?
choices: It vests the right because awareness is enough even without reliance or another trigger.
It vests the right because a plan to spend money counts as a material change of position.
It counts as requested assent even without a request or communication to either party.
It does not itself establish vesting under the selected rule.
questions.explanation: T2 specifies qualifying reliance, suit or requested communicated assent, subject to its terms. Awareness alone is different.

questions.stem: An intended beneficiary seeks payment subject to an unexcused safety-certificate condition. The certificate never issues. Under T2, what is the best response?
choices: Intended status supplies an unconditional right even when the promise is conditional.
The condition binds the promisee but does not travel with the beneficiary’s claim.
The beneficiary generally faces the condition of the promise it seeks to enforce.
Vesting of the beneficiary’s right establishes occurrence of the payment condition.
questions.explanation: An intended beneficiary enforces the bounded promise, not a newly unconditional bargain.

questions.stem: A promisor properly pays the full 3,000-dollar obligation to the entitled beneficiary. The promisee then demands another 3,000 for that same payment obligation. Under T2, what is the issue?
choices: The promisee retains the full monetary claim because it signed the original agreement.
The beneficiary and promisee each hold a separately payable copy of the same debt.
The beneficiary’s receipt leaves the original obligation unsatisfied until the promisee consents.
The second demand duplicates satisfaction of the same obligation.
questions.explanation: Multiple enforcement interests do not multiply a single satisfied obligation. Distinct recoverable losses would require separate facts.

questions.stem: Match each description to its term in the beneficiaries framework.
left: Merely gains an unintended economic advantage
choices: Promisor
Promisee
Incidental beneficiary
questions.explanation: Owes the identified performance — Promisor; Originally receives the identified promise — Promisee; Merely gains an unintended economic advantage — Incidental beneficiary. These roles or concepts must remain distinct in analysis.

questions.stem: Under T2, the restriction on altering an intended benefit after a qualifying act is described as ___.
questions.explanation: Vesting concerns limits on modification, distinct from whether the benefit was intended in the first place.

questions.stem: Sera transfers an earned payment right to a lender. Under T3, what is the transaction?
choices: Delegation of the duty to collect the receivable.
Assignment of a right.
Novation of the original services obligation.
Creation of an intended benefit in the original contract at formation.
questions.explanation: Assignment moves a right to the assignee. Neither delegation nor release follows solely from transfer of a payment claim.

questions.stem: An assigned 7,000-dollar receivable has a stipulated 500-dollar correction defense. Under T3, how much is enforceable absent other adjustments?
choices: 7,000 dollars.
6,500 dollars.
7,500 dollars.
500 dollars.
questions.explanation: The assignee takes the underlying claim subject to the applicable defense: 7,000 minus 500 equals 6,500.

questions.stem: T3's ordinary-payment rule applies. The obligor pays the assignor after effective notice of a valid assignment. What follows?
choices: It discharges the debt because payment to either claimant is enough after notice.
It discharges the debt unless the assignee also obtains the obligor’s consent.
That payment does not discharge the assigned obligation under the stated rule.
It discharges the debt until the assignee formally sues to enforce the assignment.
questions.explanation: Effective notice directs payment to the assignee under T3. A possible separate claim against the assignor is not automatic satisfaction of the assignee's right.

questions.stem: Before effective notice of a valid ordinary payment assignment, an obligor pays the assignor. No special rule is involved. Under T3, what follows?
choices: The payment discharges the obligation under the stipulated rule.
The payment leaves the debt due because the transfer itself eliminates the notice defense.
The payment discharges only if the assignee later consents to the assignor’s receipt.
The payment requires reimbursement unless the assignment was made for no consideration.
questions.explanation: The exercise explicitly protects payment to the assignor before effective notice. Special priority and statutory complications are excluded.

questions.stem: T4 permits delegation of ordinary cleaning. A qualified delegate fails; no release was agreed. What is the original contractor's position?
choices: It remains responsible for the promised cleaning.
It is discharged by the permitted transfer of performance to a qualified substitute.
It is discharged when the customer learns who will perform the delegated work.
It owes only care in selecting the delegate, instead of the promised cleaning.
questions.explanation: Permission to delegate does not extinguish the original promise. A release or novation requires additional agreement.

questions.stem: A contract specifically seeks a named artist's distinctive personal performance. Under T4, why may substitution be restricted?
choices: The existence of an earned fee makes both the payment right and duty nontransferable.
The lack of an express delegation clause bars substitution in every service agreement.
The delegate’s assumption itself creates a defense to the original performance duty.
The recipient has a substantial interest in that original personal performance.
questions.explanation: T4 recognizes a substantial personal-performance interest. That does not automatically bar a separate earned-payment assignment.

questions.stem: All necessary parties agree to substitute a new obligor and extinguish the original obligor's duty. Under T4, what does this describe?
choices: Assignment.
Intended-beneficiary agreement.
Delegation without release.
Novation.
questions.explanation: The agreement expressly adds substitution and release, the elements missing from ordinary delegation.

questions.stem: A delegate promises to perform the delegated obligation. Under T4, what must not be inferred from that assumption alone?
choices: That the delegate made a performance promise.
That the original agreement's terms remain relevant.
That the original obligor has been released.
That duplicate recovery for one loss should be avoided.
questions.explanation: An assumption may create an additional obligation without extinguishing the original one. Release requires the stipulated additional agreement.

questions.stem: Match each description to its term in the assignment framework.
choices: Assignor
Assignee
Obligor
questions.explanation: Transfers the identified contractual right — Assignor; Receives that transferred right — Assignee; Owes the underlying assigned performance — Obligor. These roles or concepts must remain distinct in analysis.

questions.stem: Under T4, authorizing another person to perform a duty is ___.
questions.explanation: Delegation concerns performance of a duty; without an additional release it leaves the original obligor responsible.

questions.stem: R1 applies. Original price is 20,000; an unreturned advance is 4,000; identical reasonable replacement is 23,000. No other loss or saving applies. What is expectation loss?
choices: 7,000 dollars.
3,000 dollars.
11,000 dollars.
27,000 dollars.
questions.explanation: Total outlay 4,000 plus 23,000 minus the original 20,000 equals 7,000. Equivalently, 23,000 minus the unpaid original balance of 16,000 gives 7,000.

questions.stem: Under R3, qualifying reliance expenditure is 5,000 and the breacher proves a 1,000-dollar loss would have occurred with full performance. What is the selected reliance measure?
choices: 5,000 dollars.
6,000 dollars.
1,000 dollars.
4,000 dollars.
questions.explanation: R3 deducts the proved losing-bargain amount from qualifying expenditure: 5,000 minus 1,000 equals 4,000.

questions.stem: A claimant paid 2,000 to the breacher and 3,000 to unrelated suppliers. No counterbenefit or offset exists. Under R4's simple advance-return alternative, what is recoverable from the retained advance?
choices: 5,000 dollars.
2,000 dollars.
3,000 dollars.
7,000 dollars.
questions.explanation: The 2,000-dollar advance is the benefit retained by the breacher. Third-party expenditure may concern reliance but is not automatically a retained benefit.

questions.stem: A replacement-cost expectation calculation already includes an unreturned advance. What happens if the same advance is added again as restitution?
choices: The sum is proper because expectation and restitution protect different named interests.
The sum is proper whenever the retained advance was paid before the breach occurred.
The sum is proper if the two components are requested as separate counts in the pleading.
The combined amount duplicates compensation for the advance.
questions.explanation: Alternative remedy labels do not authorize double recovery. Track what the expectation calculation already restores.

questions.stem: Projected event revenue is 8,000 dollars and earning it would cost 5,000. Under R2, what is the net-profit figure before other limits?
choices: 8,000 dollars.
3,000 dollars.
13,000 dollars.
5,000 dollars.
questions.explanation: Net profit subtracts the costs of earning the revenue: 8,000 minus 5,000 equals 3,000. Recoverability still requires the other R2 limits.

questions.stem: Under R2, when is the foreseeability of the type of contractual loss assessed for these exercises?
choices: When the breach occurs, using only what the breacher knows then.
When the injured party selects a substitute after learning of the breach.
At contract formation.
When the injured party first informs the other party of the resulting loss.
questions.explanation: R2 uses the formation-time perspective, including relevant known special circumstances. Later disclosure does not retroactively establish that knowledge.

questions.stem: An injured party reasonably spends 300 dollars trying to reduce breach loss, but the sensible attempt fails. Under R2, what is the best analysis?
choices: The expense is excluded because unsuccessful mitigation did not reduce the final loss.
The expense is limited to the amount of loss actually prevented by that response.
Reasonable unsuccessful mitigation expense can still qualify.
The expense qualifies only if the breacher approved the attempted response beforehand.
questions.explanation: Mitigation evaluates reasonableness in the circumstances, not success with hindsight. Eligibility still depends on the stipulated supporting facts.

questions.stem: A stated net-profit figure already deducts a particular avoided cost. What should happen to that same cost elsewhere in the R2 schedule?
choices: Do not deduct it a second time.
Deduct it again because avoided costs belong on a separate line from profit.
Add it back to the net figure and omit any corresponding savings deduction.
Deduct it again because net-profit proof and mitigation require separate reductions.
questions.explanation: The schedule must track overlap. A second subtraction of an already-netted saving understates the loss.

questions.stem: Match each description to its term in the damages measures framework.
left: Recoverable benefit conferred on the other party
choices: Expectation interest
Reliance interest
Restitution interest
questions.explanation: Promised performance position — Expectation interest; Qualifying preparatory expenditure — Reliance interest; Recoverable benefit conferred on the other party — Restitution interest. These roles or concepts must remain distinct in analysis.

questions.stem: The R2 principle limiting loss reasonably avoidable without undue burden is ___.
questions.explanation: Mitigation limits avoidable loss while allowing supported reasonable response costs; it is not a requirement of perfect hindsight.

questions.stem: R5 applies. An identified unique sculpture remains with the seller, no adequate substitute exists, and the definite order is feasible and fair. What relief has a supported basis?
choices: Only market-price damages, because the price was stated in money.
An automatic decree, because uniqueness eliminates the need for equitable discretion.
A request for specific performance, subject to the equitable requirements.
The sculpture plus its full substitute value as compensation for the same benefit.
questions.explanation: The facts support inadequacy of money and feasible specific relief. They do not erase equitable discretion or permit duplicate compensation.

questions.stem: In Cedar Hall, equivalent ordinary installation is available and Elm is reasonably hired. Under R5, what weakens forcing Alder's crew to work?
choices: The monetary price prevents specific relief even if equivalent installation were unavailable.
The presence of any services duty categorically prevents every form of equitable relief.
An adequate substitute was available; a work order also raises feasibility and supervision issues.
The absence of a liquidated-damages clause makes equitable relief unavailable.
questions.explanation: R5 requires inadequacy of money and permissible, feasible relief. Cedar obtained equivalent replacement installation, undermining that showing. A continuing work order raises supervision questions; ordinary construction is not automatically the distinctive personal service discussed in the separate prohibition.

questions.stem: R6 governs. A clause fixes 50,000 dollars for a one-hour delay; anticipated and actual loss is 20 dollars and easy to prove. No other justification exists. What is the strongest analysis?
choices: The agreed label makes the amount enforceable without comparing it with likely harm.
The signed clause controls because consent replaces the reasonableness inquiry.
The excess is enforced as consequential damages rather than tested as a fixed sum.
The amount is an unreasonably large penalty under the selected facts.
questions.explanation: R6 evaluates reasonableness, harm and proof difficulty. The label does not overcome the stated disproportion.

questions.stem: Why does R6 distinguish a liquidated-damages amount from an exclusive repair limitation?
choices: A fixed compensation measure and a restriction on available remedies raise different questions.
A repair restriction uses the same penalty test to settle every question of enforceability.
A repair restriction stipulates the amount of all losses in the same way as a fixed sum.
A reasonable fixed sum necessarily makes repair the only remaining available remedy.
questions.explanation: R6 does not resolve all limitation questions through the penalty test. The later Sales work develops those separate issues.

questions.stem: Use Cedar R02 and R08–R10, treating the preview loss as proven. Advance 6,000 plus substitute 34,000 minus price 30,000, plus response 1,000 and profit 2,000, minus saving 500 yields what?
choices: 18,500 dollars.
12,500 dollars.
6,500 dollars.
13,500 dollars.
questions.explanation: The stated components produce 12,500. The advance is counted once through total outlay, and the separate saving is subtracted once.

questions.stem: Under the Cedar record, if the 2,000-dollar preview loss is not proven but all other stipulated components remain, what is the expectation calculation?
choices: 10,500 dollars.
12,500 dollars.
6,000 dollars.
14,500 dollars.
questions.explanation: Subtract the unproved 2,000 from 12,500. Independently supported completion and response losses remain.

questions.stem: Pine received effective notice of the assigned conditional final payment, but Alder supplies no work or certificate. Under T3 and Cedar R02/R05, what follows?
choices: Effective notice makes the assigned amount payable even though completion remains absent.
Pine can demand payment because conditional rights cannot be transferred until they mature.
Alder’s transfer shifts the installation duty to Pine along with the final-payment right.
Pine’s valid assignment does not make the unfulfilled conditional payment presently due.
questions.explanation: Pine takes the actual conditional right. Notice identifies the recipient of a payment if due; it does not erase conditions or release duties.

questions.stem: Cedar requests an additional 50,000 dollars solely to punish ordinary breach, with no independent basis supplied. What does R1 support?
choices: Award the addition because a deliberate refusal itself supplies the independent punitive basis.
Reject that punitive addition while analyzing compensation separately under the stipulated rule.
Award the addition as liquidated damages because Cedar specified an exact amount in its demand.
Award the addition as disgorgement without evidence of any gain or a rule authorizing that measure.
questions.explanation: The exercise supplies no independent basis for punitive damages and no agreed amount. A supported compensatory claim remains a separate matter.

questions.stem: Match each description to its term in the equitable relief framework.
choices: Intended beneficiary
Incidental beneficiary
Assigned right
questions.explanation: Maple's expressly granted station-enforcement benefit — Intended beneficiary; Cafe's hoped-for increased trade alone — Incidental beneficiary; Pine's transferred conditional payment claim — Assigned right. These roles or concepts must remain distinct in analysis.

questions.stem: Under R5, an order to render the promised performance is called ___.
questions.explanation: Specific performance requires the stipulated equitable showing; it is not automatic upon proving breach.

decks.title: Contracts II: Performance, Breach and Remedies notecards

cards.back: A condition controls a duty; a promise commits a party to conduct. One clause can do both, but the consequences must be analyzed separately.

cards.front: Failed grant without a promise to obtain it
cards.back: Under P1, an unexcused failed grant condition keeps payment from maturing without itself proving breach.
An agreement may remain valid while a particular payment is not yet due. Do not substitute a global void-contract label.
Identify each party's ready and able offer of the agreed simultaneous performance.
Required cooperation, wrongful interference and causation of the condition's nonoccurrence.
P2 prevents abrupt restoration of a waived condition after material justified reliance under the stated facts.
P2's forfeiture excuse requires that the condition not be a material part of the exchange.
Do not replace a clear unexcused express condition with a percentage-completion argument.
Ask how the defect affects the promised benefit, compensation, forfeiture, likely cure and good faith.
P3 can require return performance while preserving an offset for defects.
Temporary withholding does not itself establish a total breach ending all remaining duties.
A 10,000-dollar due price with a stipulated 100-dollar offset leaves 9,900 dollars due.
Use the single-delivery, pre-acceptance rule with its agreement, notice and cure qualifications.
Seasonable notice plus conforming replacement within remaining contract time can make cure effective under P4.
Investigate revocation and accepted-goods remedies; initial rejection rules do not simply restart.
P4 requires the stated reasonable belief of acceptability and seasonable notice; the seller's preference is insufficient.
Compare an anxious commitment to perform with a clear refusal of material future performance.

cards.front: Conditional return at a higher price
cards.back: Willingness to perform only a different bargain need not retract refusal of the original obligation.
Check the due date, cancellation, final-treatment notice and material change before the attempted return.
A reasonable wait can be allowed; avoidable damages are not unlimited.
B2 requires reasonable grounds for insecurity, not buyer's remorse.

cards.front: What the written assurance demand seeks
cards.back: Reliable evidence of performance of the existing goods bargain, not unrelated concessions.
The reasonable response time under B2 can be shorter than thirty days.
Identify a stated services or contractual assurance rule before using a goods statute's procedure.
One concerns inability to perform; the other concerns destruction of a shared principal purpose despite possible performance.
B3 does not turn routine cost changes in an allocated fixed-price risk into automatic excuse.
Frustration requires the applicable shared principal-purpose showing, not an undisclosed hope.
Ask whether later performance still supplies materially the same exchange before asserting permanent discharge.
Identify trigger, causation, exclusions, notice, mitigation and the promised relief.
B4 applies the relief actually granted by the clause.
Fair and reasonable allocation and seasonable notice remain part of the selected excuse rule.
Analyze retained benefits separately; future-duty excuse does not automatically decide restitution.
A reciprocal party can be promisor on one duty and promisee on another.
Large economic advantage does not alone create an intended beneficiary.
A payment recipient and a delivery landmark are not equivalent manifestations of intent.
A promise to pay a named creditor in satisfaction of the promisee's debt supports intended benefit under T1.
An intended benefit can exist before an act restricts later alteration.
Subject to the stated terms, material justified reliance, suit or requested communicated assent before notice can restrict modification.

An identified right, such as an earned receivable; performance duties and release require separate analysis.

A fixed compensation formula and an exclusive repair restriction are different issues.
6,000 + 34,000 - 30,000 + 1,000 + 2,000 - 500 = 12,500 dollars under the stated assumptions.

references.title: Exercise rules — repudiation and excuse
references.body:
These are original stipulated exercise rules. They identify the framework for the fictional problems, not a universal statement of current contract law. Real primary sources appear separately below.

## B1 — Anticipatory repudiation and retraction

A clear refusal or qualifying disabling act before a material future performance is due is repudiation. Ambiguous concern alone is insufficient. A justified response can include suspending dependent performance, seeking a remedy, or awaiting performance for a reasonable time. Avoidable loss remains subject to mitigation.

A clear retraction can restore the repudiating party's rights before the next performance is due unless the injured party has cancelled, materially changed position or indicated final treatment. Include justified assurance when applicable. A binding reasonable replacement contract is a material change in these exercises. A merely exploratory quote is not automatically such a change.

## B2 — Selected goods assurance rule

Reasonable grounds for insecurity can support a written demand for adequate assurance of due performance. Pending assurance, suspension of unreturned performance must be commercially reasonable. Between merchants, use commercial standards. Failure after a justified demand to supply adequate assurance within a reasonable time, never exceeding thirty days, is repudiation. The ceiling does not guarantee thirty days when circumstances require less. Do not apply this sales procedure to services without a stated contractual or other applicable rule.

## B3 — Changed circumstances

For the services exercises, a qualifying supervening event can excuse a duty when its nonoccurrence was a basic assumption, the affected party is without fault, and the risk was not allocated to that party. Impossibility concerns objectively impossible performance; impracticability requires the extraordinary difficulty specified in the facts, not ordinary increased cost. Frustration requires substantial destruction of a principal purpose recognized by both parties. Private disappointment and ordinary market variation do not suffice.

A temporary event may suspend rather than permanently discharge a duty where later performance remains materially the same exchange. Prior breach and restitution for retained benefits require separate analysis. For the selected goods comparison, qualifying partial-capacity excuse requires fair, reasonable allocation and seasonable notice of delay or nondelivery and any estimated quota.

## B4 — Contractual allocation

Read a force majeure clause's covered event, causation, exclusions, notice and relief. Apply the relief actually agreed, not automatic total discharge. In Cedar Hall, the clause covers an official flood closure of the site, provides an extension for the closure period after prompt written notice, and excludes ordinary staffing and cost changes. No such flood or closure occurred in the base record.

## Reading anchors and limits

- [New York UCC § 2-609](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/UCC/2-609), [§ 2-610](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/UCC/2-610), [§ 2-611](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/UCC/2-611): enacted assurance, repudiation and retraction provisions for goods.
- [New York UCC § 2-615](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/UCC/2-615): selected seller excuse, allocation and notice provisions.
- [A/R Retail LLC v Hugo Boss Retail, Inc., 2021 NY Slip Op 21139](https://www.nycourts.gov/Reporter/3dseries/2021/2021_21139.htm): a New York trial-court lease dispute illustrating a restrictive impossibility analysis. It is not a controlling national rule for all transactions.

## Timeline worksheet

List formation, the threatened performance, due date, message or event, notice, response, replacement commitment and attempted retraction. At each entry state which rule becomes relevant. A later event does not automatically rewrite an earlier completed response.

references.title: Cedar Hall — model memorandum, calculation and revision rubric
references.body:
Read this after attempting the record. This is an original model using stipulated rules, not legal advice or an opinion about real parties. Other well-supported organization and phrasing can be sound. The model memorandum below is separate from the calculation schedule and rubric.

## Model memorandum

### Duties and conditions

Cedar has a strong claim that Alder repudiated a valid services agreement and remains responsible despite delegating installation. Formation and classification are stipulated in R01, so the analysis should begin with performance rather than repeat offer-and-acceptance doctrine. R02 makes conforming completion and the safety certificate express conditions of the final 24,000-dollar payment. Neither occurred. Cedar supplied required access and inspection cooperation, so the record supplies no prevention or waiver ground for excusing those conditions under P2.

This distinguishes a valid agreement from a matured payment duty. Alder's failure to install also violates its performance promise, not merely an outside condition nobody undertook to cause. No useful work or material was supplied, so P3's substantial-performance argument cannot explain away the failure. The safety condition protects a central performance interest; this is not a minor paperwork omission after completed work. Pine's assignment must be considered against that existing conditional right.

### Refusal and attempted return

Alder's October 10 message expressly refuses performance at the agreed price, both on the due date and afterward, unless Cedar adds 8,000 dollars. This concerns the agreement's central future performance and is an anticipatory repudiation under B1. It is more definite than a request to discuss staffing. Alder could argue that it remained willing to work, but willingness only on materially different price terms does not withdraw the refusal to perform the existing bargain.

Cedar promptly treated the refusal as final and reasonably sought replacement. Independently, the binding October 12 agreement with Elm materially changed Cedar's position before Alder's October 13 attempted retraction. Either established barrier defeats compulsory restoration under B1. The fact that October 28 had not yet arrived satisfies only one timing consideration; it does not eliminate the final-treatment and material-change restrictions. The replacement's reasonable price and absence of upgrades also support Cedar's response against a claim that it manufactured excessive loss.

### Excuse and responsibility

B3 does not excuse Alder's ordinary staffing and profitability choices. The site remains available, ordinary substitute workers exist, and Alder deliberately moved its crew elsewhere. The record identifies neither a qualifying impossibility nor extraordinary impracticability, and Cedar's event purpose still exists. B4's clause concerns an official flood closure, provides an extension rather than automatic cancellation, and expressly excludes ordinary staffing and cost changes. No covered closure occurred. Invoking the clause without its trigger would ignore both causation and allocated risk.

T4 permitted ordinary delegation to Birch, so delegation itself was not necessarily wrongful. It nevertheless did not extinguish Alder's installation obligation. Cedar's knowledge of Birch is not assent to release Alder, and R05 expressly denies a release. Birch's assumption may create an additional enforceable duty under the stated framework, but its failure does not immunize Alder. Any recovery for the same installation loss must be coordinated rather than multiplied merely because more than one obligor is implicated.

### Third-party positions

Maple has an intended enforcement benefit under T1 because R04 expressly gives it the activity-station promise. Its material, justified nonrefundable transport expenditure occurred before notice of modification, and no change power was reserved. Under T2 that reliance restricts alteration without consent. This establishes status and protection against modification, not an automatic award of transport damages. The assignment expressly excludes quantifying Maple's separate loss, and its 400 dollars must not be inserted into Cedar's schedule.

The cafe is in a different position. Its mention identifies a delivery landmark, and any increased trade is an incidental advantage under T1. Nothing manifests a contractual undertaking enforceable by the cafe. The possible size of its expected sales does not supply the missing intention. This conclusion addresses only contractual beneficiary status under the record, not hypothetical independent statutory or tort claims for which no facts are supplied.

Pine received a valid assignment and Cedar had notice. T3 nevertheless transfers the right Alder actually possessed, with its conditions and defenses. Alder never completed the work and no safety certificate issued, so the conditional final payment has not matured. Notice identifies the proper recipient if payment becomes due; it does not create an unconditional 24,000-dollar obligation. Cedar therefore has a strong defense to Pine's present demand without disputing the validity of the assignment itself.

### Monetary relief

Under R1, Cedar's total completion outlay is the retained 6,000-dollar advance plus the 34,000-dollar reasonable substitute, or 40,000 dollars. Compared with the original 30,000-dollar price, the replacement-related loss is 10,000 dollars. Add the separate recoverable 1,000-dollar response expense and the assumed 2,000-dollar preview net profit, then deduct the separate 500-dollar storage saving. The resulting expectation claim is 12,500 dollars. The schedule records why neither the advance nor the saving is counted twice.

R10 stipulates the preview component's recoverability for the assumed arithmetic but preserves a factual proof dispute. Cedar should support causation, formation-time knowledge, certainty and reasonable avoidance with bookings and records. If that item fails, the supported calculation becomes 10,500 dollars. Alder's certainty objection therefore affects the amount without defeating all compensation. Calling the entire claim speculative would disregard the separately established completion and response amounts.

R4 also supports considering return of the 6,000-dollar advance as an alternative because Alder supplied no counterbenefit and retained the payment after total breach. Cedar cannot add that refund to the 12,500-dollar expectation award: the advance already enters the total-outlay comparison. Reliance is another conceptual measure, but this record does not support inventing extra preparation expenditure. The alternative analysis should identify overlaps rather than construct the highest sum by combining incompatible baselines.

### Other relief and recommendation

Specific performance is weak under R5 because equivalent ordinary installation was reasonably available and Cedar obtained it. A continuing installation order also raises feasibility and supervision questions. Ordinary construction is not automatically the distinctive personal service covered by the separate prohibition; the adequate replacement is the decisive obstacle here. R1 supplies no punitive recovery for ordinary breach alone, and R11 supplies no independent basis for the requested additional 50,000 dollars. Choosing a more profitable project supports the breach narrative but does not itself create that remedy under the exercise.

Cedar should pursue the supported expectation measure with a clearly separated fallback and preserve the evidence for the contested preview loss. Its strongest analysis explains why conditions defeat Pine's current payment claim while Alder's repudiation supports Cedar's damages claim. Those conclusions concern different duties and are consistent. Before applying this framework outside the exercise, a researcher would identify the actual jurisdiction, contract terms and applicable authorities rather than presenting the stipulated rules as governing law.

## Calculation schedule

- **Retained advance: +6,000 dollars.** Part of total actual completion outlay.
- **Identical reasonable substitute: +34,000 dollars.** R08 supplies this amount; it includes no upgrade or duplicate expense.
- **Original price: −30,000 dollars.** The promised-performance baseline includes the original advance.
- **Separate response expense: +1,000 dollars.** R09 confirms that it is not included in the substitute quote.
- **Preview net profit: +2,000 dollars.** Assumed proven under R10; the costs of earning that profit are already deducted.
- **Separate storage saving: −500 dollars.** R09 confirms that it has not been deducted elsewhere.

The **expectation total is 12,500 dollars** under those expressly assumed components. **Without the disputed preview loss, it is 10,500 dollars.** The **advance-return alternative is 6,000 dollars** under R4; it is not added to expectation.

Cross-check: 34,000 substitute minus 24,000 unpaid original balance equals 10,000 replacement-related loss. Add 1,000 and 2,000, subtract 500. The advance is already reflected in the unpaid balance.

## Self-assessment rubric — 24 points

Score each dimension manually from 0 to 3: 0 absent or contradictory; 1 names the issue but omits the decisive fact; 2 applies the rule with a minor omission; 3 applies the correct stipulated rule, decisive facts and relevant counterargument or limit. This is a revision aid, not calibrated assessment or faculty approval.

- **Conditions:** Separate validity, performance promise, conditional payment and absence of prevention.
- **Repudiation and retraction:** Use the exact refusal and the October 10–13 sequence.
- **Excuse:** Address ordinary risk and the flood clause's trigger and limited remedy.
- **Delegation:** Distinguish permitted substitution, assumption and actual release.
- **Third-party rights:** Distinguish Maple, cafe and Pine without enlarging any promise.
- **Expectation:** Show 12,500 and explain advance and savings treatment.
- **Alternatives and proof:** Show 10,500 and 6,000 separately; identify uncertainty and overlap.
- **Other relief and writing:** Evaluate equitable and punitive requests; organize rules, facts and application clearly.

## Revision example

Weak draft: “Pine owns the contract, so Cedar owes 24,000 dollars.”

Revised: “Pine holds Alder's assigned final-payment right under R05, but T3 preserves the completion and certification conditions. Neither occurred under R02, and Cedar did not prevent them. Effective notice changes the recipient of a payment that becomes due; it does not make that conditional payment presently enforceable.”

## Changed-fact checks

Earlier retraction: check clarity, readiness, any justified assurance, and whether cancellation, final treatment or material change already occurred. The changed problem removes the stated barriers; do not invent a replacement commitment.

Actual novation: an effective agreed substitution and release changes the original obligor's responsibility under T4. Mere delegation in the base record did not.

Covered closure: apply the clause's duration and notice requirements. Its stated remedy is an extension, not automatic price cancellation.

Storage already netted: omit a second 500-dollar deduction. Holding every other number unchanged would produce 13,000 dollars; the altered definition of the net-profit figure must be made explicit.

references.title: Exercise rules — conditions and performance
references.body:
These original numbered rules are stipulated teaching assumptions for this course. They are not quotations, enacted law, a national contract code or the rules of a real jurisdiction. Apply them when a lesson or question invokes them. Research actual governing law before transferring an analysis to a real dispute.

## P1 — Promises and conditions

A promise commits a party to conduct. A condition is an uncertain event whose occurrence, unless excused, controls a duty. Nonoccurrence of a condition is not itself breach unless a party also promised the event or relevant conduct. Clear express conditions require their specified event. Doubtful language is interpreted as a promise rather than an express condition when the latter construction would create forfeiture. Concurrent duties ordinarily require each party's ready and able tender. Separate whether a duty is due from whether another promise was broken.

## P2 — Excusing a condition

A party may not rely on nonoccurrence it wrongfully caused by preventing required cooperation. A clear waiver can excuse a condition protecting the waiving party. Reinstatement before reliance requires reasonable notice and an opportunity to comply; a party cannot restore a waived condition after material justified reliance under these exercises. Disproportionate forfeiture may support excuse only where the event is not a material part of the agreed exchange. An essential safety condition is not erased simply because compliance is expensive.

## P3 — Services and constructive conditions

Unless the agreement or problem states otherwise, substantial performance satisfies a constructive condition of return performance while leaving damages for defects. Assess materiality through deprivation of the expected benefit, adequacy of compensation, forfeiture, likely cure and good faith. A material uncured failure may justify suspension. Treat remaining duties as discharged only when the facts establish a total breach; timing, cure prospects and the bargain's purpose matter. A minor compensable defect ordinarily supports damages rather than abandonment of remaining duties.

Use reasonable correction cost where stipulated appropriate. If correction is grossly disproportionate to its benefit, consider diminution in value under the selected facts, including the agreed feature's special purpose. There is no blanket permission to substitute something the provider considers equally good.

## P4 — Selected goods comparison

For a single delivery before acceptance, a nonconforming tender permits timely rejection and notice under the exercise facts, subject to contract terms and cure. A seller giving seasonable notice may make a conforming delivery within unexpired contract time. A further reasonable cure period can apply when the original tender was reasonably believed acceptable and notice is seasonable. Acceptance, revocation of acceptance and installment deliveries have separate requirements; do not extend this simplified starting rule to them.

## Reading anchors

- [National Fuel Gas Distribution Corp. v Hartford Fire Insurance Co., 2005 NY Slip Op 52274(U)](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2005/2005_52274.htm): trial-court discussion of conditions and interpretation, quoting higher New York authority.
- [Jacob & Youngs, Inc. v Kent, 230 NY 239 (1921)](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/archives/jacob_kent.htm): Court of Appeals opinion and dissent concerning construction performance and the appropriate defect measure.
- [New York UCC § 2-601](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/UCC/2-601) and [§ 2-508](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/UCC/2-508): enacted sales provisions on nonconforming tender and cure.

## Analysis worksheet

| Question | What to record |
|---|---|
| What is due? | Identify the precise promise and its obligor. |
| What controls it? | Identify an express or constructive condition, if any. |
| What happened? | Use dates, inspection evidence and communications. |
| Is nonoccurrence excused? | Specify prevention, waiver or forfeiture facts. |
| What response follows? | Separate payment, offset, suspension and discharge. |

references.title: Cedar Hall — complete fictional record and assignment
references.body:
This is an original fictional closed-universe exercise. Cedar Hall is a community organization, not a jurisdiction. Apply P1–P4, B1–B4, T1–T4 and R1–R6 as stipulated teaching rules. There are no hidden documents or unstated legal authorities to discover. All dates occur in the same fictional year.

## R01 — Parties and valid agreement

Cedar Hall contracts with Alder Works on September 1 for installation of temporary interior exhibition fixtures, completed by October 28 for an October 29 preview and October 30 community event. Formation, capacity, writing and interpretation are undisputed. Treat the transaction as services. Alder's work is ordinary installation; no named artisan's unique personal performance is promised.

## R02 — Price and conditions

The price is 30,000 dollars. Cedar pays a 6,000-dollar advance on September 1. The remaining 24,000 dollars is expressly due only after Alder completes conforming installation and Cedar's inspector issues a safety certificate. Cedar must provide access and timely inspection. Cedar satisfies every cooperation duty. No installation work or useful material is ever provided by Alder or its delegate, and no certificate issues.

## R03 — Event and known loss

At formation Cedar gives Alder the event schedule, historical net-profit records and the October 28 installation deadline. Alder acknowledges that missing that deadline may force cancellation of the preview session on October 29. The main event can still proceed if replacement installation is finished on October 30, but that later completion cannot preserve the preview.

## R04 — Intended benefit and nearby trade

The agreement expressly grants Maple Youth Group the right to enforce Alder's promise to install an accessible activity station as part of the work. Maple receives the promise and justifiably pays a nonrefundable 400-dollar participant-transport charge on October 2 before any notice of modification. No power to change Maple's right is reserved. The contract mentions a nearby cafe only as a landmark for delivery drivers. Increased cafe sales are anticipated by the cafe alone; no enforcement right or promised payment to the cafe is stated.

For this exercise, analyze Maple's status and modification protection, not a monetary claim for its transport expense. That charge is not part of Cedar's damages schedule.

## R05 — Delegation and assignment

Alder may delegate ordinary installation to qualified crews. On October 3 it hires Birch Crew, which assumes the installation duty but later does no work. Cedar knows of the delegation but never agrees to release Alder. Separately, Alder validly assigns its conditional 24,000-dollar final-payment right to Pine Finance. Cedar receives effective notice on October 4. The assignment does not remove any contract condition or defense, and no priority or consumer-law complication applies.

## R06 — Allocation clause

The agreement grants an extension for an official flood closure of the site lasting as long as that closure, provided prompt written notice is given. It excludes ordinary staffing shortages and cost changes. There is no flood, government closure, destruction of the site or other extraordinary event. Ordinary substitute workers are available. Alder instead moves its regular crew to a more profitable project.

## R07 — Clear refusal

On October 10 Alder writes: “We will not perform the Cedar job by October 28 or later at the agreed price. We have moved our crew to another project. We will return only if you pay an additional 8,000 dollars.” It keeps the 6,000-dollar advance and supplies nothing of value. Cedar promptly says it treats the refusal as final and seeks reasonable replacement.

## R08 — Replacement and attempted retraction

After comparing three qualified bids, Cedar signs a binding, reasonable 34,000-dollar replacement agreement with Elm Installers on October 12. It purchases the same promised work without upgrades. Elm can finish October 30 but cannot save the October 29 preview. On October 13 Alder offers to perform the original agreement at the original price. Cedar has already committed to Elm; Alder knows the replacement is binding.

## R09 — Response expense and savings

Cedar reasonably incurs a separate 1,000-dollar emergency coordination and transport expense because of Alder's breach. It is not included in Elm's 34,000-dollar quote. Cedar also saves a 500-dollar storage charge because replacement fixtures arrive later. That charge would otherwise have been paid in addition to the original price and is not already deducted in any other figure. For the assumed calculation, these amounts and their recoverability or deductibility are undisputed.

## R10 — Preview loss and disputed proof

Cedar claims 2,000 dollars of net profit lost on the cancelled preview. Its schedule already deducts all variable preview costs from projected revenue. The separate 500-dollar storage saving in R09 is not part of that net-profit computation. Cedar supplies historical records and bookings; Alder challenges whether they sufficiently establish attendance for this year's preview.

For the requested assumed calculation, treat the 2,000-dollar net loss as caused, foreseeable at formation, reasonably certain and not reasonably avoidable. In the memorandum, also state the result if Cedar fails to prove that item. Do not pretend the stipulation settles the real evidentiary disagreement.

## R11 — Requested relief

Cedar requests expectation compensation, or alternatively return of its 6,000-dollar advance. It has received no refund, no useful counterbenefit and no payment satisfying either measure. There are no liquidated-damages, exclusive-remedy or consequential-loss-exclusion terms. Cedar also asks whether a court should force Alder's crew to work and whether an extra 50,000 dollars can punish Alder for choosing a more profitable job. No independent wrong or other basis for punitive damages is supplied.

## R12 — Closed record and scope

No party has paid Pine the final balance. Alder has not substantially performed. No one prevented inspection. Cedar has not released Alder or agreed to an increased price. Do not import a goods statute as the governing services rule. Identify relevant primary-law analogies only as further research, not as an unstated source of new facts or exercise rules.

## Deliverables

1. A 900–1,200-word objective breach memorandum identifying conditions, repudiation, retraction, excuse, delegation, Maple's and the cafe's status, and Pine's conditional right.
2. A separate damages table showing the expectation calculation, the alternative advance return, the no-double-recovery explanation and the result without the disputed preview loss.
3. A short assessment of specific performance and punitive recovery.
4. A revision note identifying one corrected assumption or calculation and one strengthened counterargument.

Write your own analysis before opening the model reference. The app quizzes are objective practice; this memorandum and its 24-point rubric are manual self-assessment.

## Changed-fact exercises

- Retraction reaches Cedar October 11, before any final-treatment communication or binding replacement. What further facts determine restoration?
- All necessary parties sign a clear agreement substituting Birch and releasing Alder before Birch's failure. How does responsibility change?
- An official flood closure occurs and Alder satisfies the clause's notice terms. What relief does the clause actually provide?
- Cedar's storage saving is already included in the stipulated net-profit figure. How must the arithmetic change to avoid a duplicate deduction?

references.title: Exercise rules — remedy measures and limits
references.body:
These original rules stipulate the framework for the course's calculations. They are not legal advice or a substitute for a jurisdiction's law. Questions state when supporting evidence is assumed. A calculation under assumed facts is not a finding that disputed facts are proven.

## R1 — Expectation

Compare the injured party's position after breach with promised performance: loss in value plus recoverable other loss minus costs or losses avoided. For total abandonment before any useful work, an owner's reasonable replacement measure is total completion outlay, including retained advances, less the original contract price, plus supported additional loss less savings. Equivalently, replacement cost less the unpaid original balance accounts for the retained advance already. Do not add that advance twice.

The course excludes punitive damages for ordinary breach without an independently supported basis, and the fictional record supplies none. Do not automatically award the breacher's savings to the claimant.

## R2 — Limits and evidence

Each item must result from breach, satisfy the stipulated foreseeability requirement at formation, and have a reasonably certain amount. Reasonably avoidable loss is excluded; reasonable unsuccessful mitigation expense may qualify. Avoided costs reduce recovery once. Net profit excludes the costs required to earn the revenue. Identify which savings are already included in a supplied net figure.

## R3 — Reliance alternative

Reasonable, foreseeable, supported expenditure in preparation for or performance of the agreement may be considered as an alternative measure, less any loss the breaching party proves with reasonable certainty the claimant would have suffered from full performance. Do not add the same expenditure again as restitution or expectation.

## R4 — Restitution alternative

For the stipulated injured party after a total breach, assess the recoverable benefit conferred on the breaching party, subject to applicable offsets. An unreturned advance with no counterbenefit is the simple example. Expenses paid to unrelated third parties are not automatically benefits retained by the defendant. This alternative does not cover the fully performed fixed-price case in which only money payment remains due. It does not authorize a breaching party's unrestricted recovery or erase a valid price term.

## R5 — Equitable relief

Specific performance requires a supported inadequacy of money, sufficiently definite and feasible relief, and satisfaction of the stipulated equitable considerations. Unique goods or other proper circumstances can support the selected goods comparison. The exercises do not compel personal services or assume a negative restraint is automatically permissible. No duplicate recovery of the same promised benefit is allowed.

## R6 — Agreed damages

For these exercises, assess a liquidated amount against anticipated or actual harm, difficulty of proving loss and adequacy of other relief. An unreasonably large amount is a penalty. A label does not decide validity. Remedy limitations raise separate issues; their enforceability is not presumed from the presence of a damages clause. No such agreed amount or limitation appears in Cedar Hall's base record.

## Reading anchors

- [New York UCC § 2-712](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/UCC/2-712) and [§ 2-715](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/UCC/2-715): cover and additional sales losses.
- [St. Lawrence Factory Stores v Ogdensburg Bridge & Port Authority, 2009 NY Slip Op 07454](https://www.nycourts.gov/Reporter/3dseries/2009/2009_07454.htm): New York Court of Appeals opinion recognizing a reliance alternative and a proved losing-bargain deduction.
- [St. Lawrence Factory Stores, 2014 NY Slip Op 07035](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2014/2014_07035.htm): later appellate review of the remand evidence and the losing-bargain deduction; distinguish an available claim from a supported amount.
- [New York UCC § 2-716](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/UCC/2-716) and [§ 2-718(1)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/UCC/2-718): selected equitable and agreed-damages comparisons.

## Calculation worksheet

| Entry | Required explanation |
|---|---|
| Baseline | Whose promised position, and which measure? |
| Payment | Is it already counted in total outlay or unpaid balance? |
| Additional loss | Causation, foreseeability, certainty and response evidence. |
| Savings | Whether already deducted from a net figure. |
| Alternative | Separate calculation and identification of overlap. |
| Uncertainty | Conditional result if a disputed component is not established. |

references.title: Exercise rules — beneficiaries and transfers
references.body:
Apply these stipulated teaching rules to the fictional exercises. They do not decide every state's beneficiary doctrine or the special statutory rules governing secured receivables, consumer obligations, negotiable instruments or public projects.

## T1 — Intended and incidental benefits

An intended beneficiary may enforce a promise where recognition fits manifested contractual intention and the performance either satisfies the promisee's payment obligation to that person or is intended to confer the promised benefit on that person. A merely incidental economic advantage is insufficient. Naming a person is relevant evidence, not a universal requirement or guarantee. Read an applicable enforcement limitation in context.

## T2 — Changes and defenses

Absent a reserved power of change, an intended beneficiary's qualifying act before notice of modification restricts change without consent: material justified reliance, suit, or requested assent communicated to promisor or promisee. Awareness alone does not satisfy this exercise rule. The beneficiary remains subject to applicable conditions and defenses of the promise enforced. Payment satisfying the same obligation is counted once; multiple claimants cannot duplicate recovery for one injury.

## T3 — Assignment of rights

A valid assignment transfers the identified right to the assignee. Ordinary payment rights are transferable unless an applicable rule or effective restriction controls. A transfer that materially changes the obligor's duty or materially increases its burden or risk is restricted. Interpret restrictions rather than assuming identical effects for all wording.

The assignee ordinarily takes the underlying claim subject to applicable contract defenses. For these ordinary-payment exercises, payment to the assignor before effective notice discharges the debt, while payment to the assignor after effective notice does not discharge the assigned obligation. The facts exclude priority disputes and statutory proof-request complications. A transferred conditional payment is still conditional.

## T4 — Delegation and novation

Ordinary performance may be delegated unless barred by agreement or a substantial interest in the original promisor's personal performance or control. Permitted delegation alone does not release the original obligor. A delegate's assumption may create an additional enforceable duty under the stated arrangement, without eliminating the delegator's duty. A novation substituting obligors requires the necessary parties' agreement to the substitution and release. Knowledge of a subcontractor is not itself that agreement.

## Reading anchors

- [DeLine v CitiCapital Commercial Corp., 2005 NY Slip Op 09995](https://www.nycourts.gov/Reporter/3dseries/2005/2005_09995.htm): New York intermediate appellate beneficiary decision.
- [Logan-Baldwin v L.S.M. General Contractors, Inc., 2012 NY Slip Op 03046](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2012/2012_03046.htm): New York intermediate appellate decision discussing intended-benefit evidence and an incomplete record.
- [New York UCC § 2-210](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/UCC/2-210): enacted goods provision distinguishing assignment and delegation. Its Article 9 cross-reference marks additional legal territory beyond these exercises.

## Rights-and-duties worksheet

| Role | Inquiry |
|---|---|
| Promisor | Who owes this particular performance? |
| Promisee | Who originally received this promise? |
| Beneficiary | What promised benefit and enforcement intent support the claim? |
| Assignor and assignee | Which existing right was transferred? |
| Delegator and delegate | Who must perform, and who remains liable? |
| Alleged released party | What actual agreement extinguishes the former duty? |
